items.title: Makkah alliance military chiefs vow to ‘immediately’ translate commitments into effective military cooperation: ISPR
items.description: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have expressed a shared determination to “immediately translate” their commitments under the Makkah Defence Alliance into effective military cooperation, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Saturday. The commitment was made at a meeting of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir and the chiefs of general staff of Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Riyadh on Friday. The meeting took place against the backdrop of heightened security concerns in the kingdom, with the Houthis and the Yemeni government engaged in renewed fighting . The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade targeting Saudi Arabia and attacked ships in the Red Sea, while also carrying out attacks in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Earlier, the Foreign Office (FO) had said the three countries were considering a meeting of their military chiefs to discuss ways to assist Riyadh under the Makkah Defence Alliance. According to the ISPR, the participants discussed measures to advance cooperation among their armed forces, including enhanced intelligence sharing, military coordination and integration of capabilities. The measures would help strengthen deterrence and collective defence, the military’s media wing said. The participants also reviewed the security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia and strongly “resented” attacks targeting the holy city of Makkah as well as civilian and economic infrastructure. They appreciated the vigilance and professionalism of the Saudi armed forces in ensuring the safety of the people and security of the kingdom, according to the ISPR. The military chiefs further affirmed their commitment to collective defence, which, the ISPR said, demonstrated the resolve of the three countries to defend Saudi Arabia’s security, sovereignty and territorial integrity. The ISPR added that the Riyadh meeting reflected the strength of the defence partnership among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, as well as their shared determination to implement the commitments under the tripartite defence agreement. The participants also commended the longstanding relations and mutual trust between the three countries and their armed forces. Kingdom ‘welcomed’ outcomes of meeting Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, in a post on X, said that he and CDF Field Marshal Munir “welcomed the outcomes” of the chiefs of staff meeting held under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. Prince Khalid said they discussed the “heinous attacks” targeting the holy city of Makkah as well as on the kingdom’s civilian and economic infrastructure. He said the two sides affirmed their continued joint efforts to confront the attacks in accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. The Makkah alliance was signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah on Aug 7 and the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee was subsequently held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where the three countries agreed to establish a permanent secretariat in Riyadh and decided that Pakistan would provide the secretary general for its first three-year term. Pakistan appointed retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood as the alliance’s first secretary general , taking another step towards putting the institutional structure of the pact in place. The earlier New York ministerial meeting indicated that the three governments wanted the military chiefs to examine practical options. Therefore, the Riyadh meeting was expected to begin that process, although any decision on specific deployments or military assistance would depend on the Saudi requirement and the agreement reached by the three sides. Turkiye has already signalled its willingness to address Saudi military requirements, with Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan saying last week that Ankara was ready to help with “military needs, especially on some technical issues”. Pakistan has also repeatedly affirmed its commitment to the agreement.

items.title: Décès de Sidya Touré : Dr Ousmane Kaba rend hommage à un « grand frère » de près de trente ans
items.description: La disparition de l’ancien Premier ministre guinéen Sidya Touré à Paris suscite de nombreuses réactions au sein de la classe politique guinéenne. Parmi les témoignages les plus personnels figure celui du Dr Ousmane Kaba, leader du PADES, ancien ministre et député, qui dit perdre, au-delà d’un compagnon de lutte, « un grand frère ». Sidya Touré est décédé à Paris le 25 septembre 2026, à l’âge de 81 ans, selon plusieurs sources guinéennes. Ancien Premier ministre sous la présidence de Lansana Conté et président de l’Union des forces républicaines (UFR), il a marqué plusieurs décennies de la vie politique nationale. Dans son témoignage, Dr Ousmane Kaba revient sur une relation vieille de près de trente ans. Leur parcours commun remonte notamment à 1998, lorsque Sidya Touré dirigeait le gouvernement guinéen. Le Dr Kaba, alors membre de l’équipe gouvernementale, affirme avoir travaillé à ses côtés sur les questions économiques. Il garde notamment en mémoire une phrase que lui aurait adressée l’ancien Premier ministre : « Quand le docteur Ousmane Kaba parle d’économie, il faut appliquer ce qu’il dit. » Une déclaration que l’ancien ministre interprète comme le témoignage d’une confiance professionnelle et d’une estime réciproque. Après leur passage au gouvernement, les deux hommes ont poursuivi leur engagement politique et participé à la création de l’UFR. Au fil des années, explique Ousmane Kaba, leur relation aurait dépassé le cadre strictement politique pour devenir une véritable relation fraternelle, fondée sur le respect, la confiance et la fidélité. Pour le leader du PADES, la disparition de Sidya Touré constitue ainsi une double perte. « Personnellement, je perds un aîné, un compagnon de route et un grand frère » , écrit-il, rappelant que près de trois décennies de souvenirs, de travail et de fraternité ne sauraient s’effacer avec la disparition de l’ancien chef du gouvernement. Dans son hommage, Ousmane Kaba salue également l’engagement de Sidya Touré au service de la République et son attachement à la Guinée, tout en rappelant son engagement politique en faveur du dialogue et de la paix. Il adresse enfin ses condoléances à la famille du défunt, à ses proches, à ses compagnons politiques ainsi qu’au peuple de Guinée, avant de conclure par une prière musulmane : « Qu’Allah, dans Son infinie miséricorde, lui pardonne ses péchés, l’accueille dans Son vaste Paradis et donne à sa famille la force et la patience nécessaires pour traverser cette terrible épreuve. » « Repose en paix, Grand frère Sidya. La Guinée se souviendra de ton engagement. Et moi, je n’oublierai jamais le respect, la considération et la confiance que tu m’as toujours témoignés » , conclut-il.

items.title: Rule of law must be protected – GBA condemns EOCO action against Baffour Awuah
items.description: The Ghana Bar Association (GBA) has expressed concern over the Economic and Organised Crime Office’s (EOCO) attempted arrest of Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah at the Accra High Court Complex. The statement signed by GBA President Mrs Efua Ghartey and National Secretary Kwaku Gyau Baffour condemned the incident that occurred on September 23, 2026, when Mr Baffour Awuah was at the court premises to represent a client in his capacity as a lawyer. The Association said it had also taken note of videos circulating online showing another lawyer, Enoch Anhwere Afoakwa, complaining of being assaulted by a woman later confirmed by EOCO to be its officer. The GBA stressed that while no individual is above the law, enforcement action involving lawyers must respect constitutional guarantees, applicable legal procedures and the independence of the legal profession. It warned that actions perceived as circumventing those safeguards could create an atmosphere of intimidation and have a chilling effect on lawyers performing their professional duties. “Lawyers play a critical role in the administration of justice and the protection of the rights of citizens,” the Association said. It added that any action that appears to interfere with lawyers’ ability to represent clients through “arbitrary or irregular measures” risks undermining public confidence in the justice system and the rule of law. The GBA referred to concerns previously raised by its President, Mrs Efua Ghartey, about incidents involving lawyers while performing their professional duties. At the GBA’s 2025 annual conference in Wa, Mrs Ghartey said: “The Bar must never waver in its role as the voice of the voiceless. Unfortunately, recent Incidents affecting lawyers in the performance of their duties have left much to be desired.” She also said lawyers should be free to defend clients of their choice without being heckled, warning that such conduct could stifle the provision of pro bono services. At the Association’s virtual mid-year conference on June 5, 2026, Mrs Ghartey also raised concerns over the treatment of former GBA Vice President Justice Minka Premo and a young female associate who had gone to defend a client at BNI. According to her, the two were arrested and detained overnight, with the female lawyer separated from her baby. The GBA is now calling on EOCO and other state institutions to ensure that their actions comply with due process, fairness and respect for the rights of all persons involved. “The rule of law demands not only that justice be done, but that it be seen to be done,” the Association said. It added that the independence of the legal profession remains a cornerstone of democratic society and must be protected.

items.title: I didn’t concentrate road projects in Southeast — Umahi
items.description: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki ABAKALIKI — Minister of Works, Senator David Umahi, has denied allegations that he has concentrated federal road projects in the South-East geopolitical zone, saying projects under his ministry are distributed across the country in line with approvals by President Bola Tinubu. Umahi spoke while inspecting the Trans-Sahara Highway, which starts from Afikpo in Ebonyi State, traverses Ador in Benue State, Nsukka, parts of Kogi State and terminates at Owete Bridge in the Federal Capital Territory. The minister directed the contractor handling the project to work on three sections simultaneously to accelerate construction. He also assured that he would cross the Ador Bridge during his next inspection visit to the project. Umahi said allegations on social media that he had cornered road projects to the South-East were unfounded, insisting that the distribution of projects was based on federal government approvals. “They want to gag me on social media when they say I cornered all the road projects to the South-East. That is very wonderful. But we have publication of all projects ongoing. So, I’m not on my own. The President is my boss,” he said. He added: “So, where will he be when I corner our projects to the South-East?” The minister said the South-East deserved infrastructure development, but argued that the region was not being given preferential treatment at the expense of other parts of the country. “Some people are not happy that, for the first time, South-East people are getting their own share of the infrastructure of our nation. And so, there is nothing like that,” he said. “I have always said that the South-East, in terms of infrastructure development, may not be first or second or third. Definitely, they will not be the last.” Umahi also defended the administration’s approach to infrastructure financing, arguing that borrowing for productive infrastructure could be justified where the funds were deployed to projects capable of generating long-term economic benefits. He cited the Ebonyi State ring road, saying the state borrowed $150 million during his tenure as governor to construct 199 kilometres of the road. “We borrowed because we knew what to do with the money. When you don’t know what to do with the money, you go and say you are saving and they want people to clap for you. What kind of economics is that?” he said. Umahi argued that the cost of constructing the project today would be significantly higher, adding that infrastructure financing should be assessed against the economic benefits of timely investment. “I don’t believe in saving money, saving food when the people are hungry,” he said. The minister said the federal government had also combined naira funding with foreign financing for some of its legacy infrastructure projects. “All the four legacy projects, for example, each of the projects has been 30 per cent funded in naira by the Federal Government. The other 70 per cent is foreign financing,” he said. Umahi dismissed claims that the administration had abandoned existing roads in favour of constructing new ones, saying several of the projects involved the expansion and rehabilitation of existing road corridors. “And so, when people say, well, you have left all the existing roads to build new ones, that is not true. We came through existing roads that were expanded,” he said. He also defended the administration’s infrastructure and economic reform agenda, saying the projects being executed were intended to address longstanding infrastructure deficits. Umahi, who is a member of the All Progressives Congress, also urged residents of the South-East and other parts of the country to support Tinubu’s administration. He said continued support would enable the government to complete ongoing projects and sustain its reform programme. The minister further cited Nigeria’s foreign exchange reserves, which he said were about $55 billion, as an indication of developments under the administration. The post I didn’t concentrate road projects in Southeast — Umahi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Diphtheria: Death toll hits 31 as cases rise to 469 in Plateau
items.description: By Golok Nanmwa The death toll from the diphtheria outbreak in Plateau State has risen to 31, with 469 suspected cases recorded across 10 Local Government Areas of the state. Worried by the development, the Plateau State Government has activated the Incident Management System, IMS, to strengthen coordination of the response, while Dr. Maren Job Damala has been appointed Incident Manager to lead efforts to contain the outbreak. Commissioner for Health, Dr. Nicholas Ba’amlong, disclosed this on Friday during a press briefing on the outbreak in Jos. Ba’amlong said, “Although the state recorded sporadic suspected cases earlier in the year, the situation became a significant public health concern from August. “Of the 469 suspected cases recorded so far, three have been laboratory-confirmed, while 31 deaths have unfortunately been recorded.” Giving a breakdown of the cases, he said, “Jos North has recorded the highest number of suspected cases with 370, followed by Wase with 29, Jos South 22, Barkin Ladi and Mangu with 16 cases each, Pankshin five, Kanam and Mikang four each, Shendam two and Bassa one case. On the response to the outbreak, the Commissioner said, “The state’s response has been comprehensive and multi-faceted, involving the engagement and sensitisation of community leaders, intensified active case search and contact tracing, community diagnosis and treatment of mild cases, as well as the provision of treatment commodities to Plateau State Specialist Hospital and Jos University Teaching Hospital for the isolation and management of severe cases.” He added, “Teachers from public and private schools in Jos North have also been trained on early detection of diphtheria and appropriate response measures.” On vaccination, Ba’amlong said, “More than 160,000 children have been reached with diphtheria and tetanus vaccines, while over 30,000 children have received Pentavalent vaccines. “However, the state currently has a deficit of 250,000 doses required to cover the remaining parts of Jos North and other affected Local Government Areas.” He said, “Media engagement, production and airing of public enlightenment jingles, as well as printing of Information, Education and Communication materials, are also being utilised to improve awareness, promote early presentation for treatment and encourage community participation in the response.” On the activation of the Incident Management System, the Commissioner said, “The Incident Management System has been formally activated, with Dr. Maren Job Damala appointed as Incident Manager to coordinate the state’s intensified response to the outbreak.” According to him, “The Incident Manager will coordinate response activities across sectors and partners, liaise with relevant government agencies and stakeholders, ensure timely implementation of response strategies, monitor and evaluate containment activities, facilitate resource mobilisation and deployment, and ensure effective communication and dissemination of information to the public.” Ba’amlong said, “The next phase of the response will include continued active case search and contact tracing, possible intensification of vaccination and community sensitisation, regular monitoring and evaluation, as well as coordination meetings among stakeholders to review progress and address emerging challenges.” Describing diphtheria, he said, “Diphtheria is a highly infectious acute bacterial disease that can affect all age groups, although available data show that children aged two to 14 years are the most affected and more likely to present with severe forms of the disease.” He listed the symptoms as “cough, sneezing, fever, sore throat, white or greyish patches at the back of the throat, difficulty in breathing, neck swelling and, occasionally, skin rash.” The Commissioner urged parents and caregivers to ensure that their children were fully vaccinated, saying, “Diphtheria is a vaccine-preventable disease.” He advised residents to “practise good hygiene, including regular handwashing, avoid close contact with persons showing symptoms, use face masks in crowded areas or when interacting with symptomatic persons, and seek immediate medical attention where diphtheria is suspected.” Ba’amlong further urged the public to promptly report suspected cases, saying, “Members of the public should report suspected cases to their Local Government Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers, He stressed that “early reporting remains critical to containing the outbreak.” The Commissioner commended the State and Local Government Rapid Response Teams, saying, “I appreciate the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, National Primary Health Care Development Agency, WHO, UNICEF, Red Cross, FHI360 through the EPiC Project, Save the Children, Life Helpers, Chigari Foundation and other partners for their support.” He also expressed appreciation to Governor Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang, saying, “I appreciate the Governor of Plateau State for his continued support and leadership, and call on partners, community leaders, parents, health workers and residents to sustain their cooperation with government as the state works to contain the outbreak and protect the health of its citizens.” The post Diphtheria: Death toll hits 31 as cases rise to 469 in Plateau appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 950,000 barrels of Sankofa crude head to TOR as GNPC deepens domestic refining
items.description: The Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) has supplied approximately 950,000 barrels of Sankofa crude oil to the Tema Oil Refinery (TOR), deepening the link between Ghana’s upstream petroleum production and domestic refining. The crude was delivered aboard the Sonangol Cazenga and received at TOR under a commercial arrangement between the two state institutions. The milestone was marked by an inspection of the vessel by a team jointly led by GNPC Chief Executive Kwame Ntow Amoah and TOR Managing Director Edmond Kombat. For GNPC, the transaction provides an opportunity to create a dependable domestic market for Ghana’s crude while supporting efforts to process more of the country’s petroleum resources locally. Speaking at the ceremony, Mr Amoah said the arrangement reflects the President’s vision of strengthening linkages between the upstream and downstream petroleum sectors. He said it would support domestic refining and help retain more value from Ghana’s petroleum resources within the local economy. “The supply of Sankofa crude to TOR on commercial terms represents more than a transaction between two state institutions. It is an opportunity to take a Ghanaian resource, process more of it in Ghana, and create value across our own petroleum industry,” he said. Mr Amoah said a dependable national refinery would provide GNPC with a ready domestic market for its crude and lay the foundation for a sustainable commercial relationship between the two institutions. “We don’t have to look far afield for buyers. We know there is a dependable buyer for our oil in-country, and it is a commercial arrangement,” he said. He disclosed that GNPC currently has approximately eight to ten similar crude cargoes available annually. While some of these volumes are committed under existing arrangements, he said increased production could create opportunities to supply additional cargoes to TOR over time. “We are seeing an uptick in production, and we are continuing with our aggressive exploration efforts, including our onshore pursuit of the Voltaian Basin exploratory programme, to increase production and sustain the supply of crude to the refinery,” Mr Amoah said. Mr Kombat confirmed that the Sankofa cargo was fully paid for through a Letter of Credit accepted by GNPC, with no debt exposure arising from the transaction. The Sankofa crude is also considered suitable feedstock for TOR as the refinery rebuilds its operating capacity. Mr Kombat described it as light and sweet crude, with the potential to yield products including gasoline, gasoil, aviation fuel and LPG. Beyond crude supply, GNPC and TOR are exploring additional areas of collaboration. Mr Amoah said discussions are underway on supplying natural gas to support TOR’s refinery operations. For GNPC, the Sankofa crude arrangement demonstrates the potential of commercially sustainable collaboration between national institutions while creating a platform that can expand alongside Ghana’s growing upstream production. “We believe the collaboration with TOR will continue to grow stronger,” Mr Amoah said. GNPC said it remains committed to increasing Ghana’s petroleum production and working with partners across the value chain to ensure the country derives greater and lasting value from its oil and gas resources.

items.title: Obi rallies support for NDC in Delta
items.description: Former presidential candidate of the Labour Party, Peter Obi, has called for unity, improved security and a shift from consumption to production as part of efforts to create jobs and reduce poverty in Nigeria. Obi stated this in a post on his X platform on Saturday while recounting his visit to Delta State on Thursday, September 24. He said he joined the National Democratic Congress (NDC) governorship candidate in the state, Deacon Chris Iyovwaye, other candidates, party leaders and members at the inauguration of the party’s campaign office in Asaba. According to Obi, the event provided another opportunity to communicate the party’s message and its commitment to what he described as a better Nigeria. He said the country must unite, strengthen its security architecture and move from a consumption-driven economy to one focused on production. “We must unite, secure our dear nation, and move it from consumption to production, create jobs, and pull our people out of poverty,” Obi said. He thanked Iyovwaye, other party leaders and members in Delta State for their commitment to the party’s campaign and what he described as the development of the state and Nigeria. Obi also expressed appreciation to residents of the state for the reception and hospitality extended to him and his delegation. “A New Nigeria is Possible, and Nigeria will be OK,” he said. The post Obi rallies support for NDC in Delta appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: APM asks Tinubu to quit 2027 race, back Makinde
items.description: ABUJA — The Allied Peoples Movement (APM) has urged President Bola Tinubu to withdraw from the 2027 presidential race and support its candidate, Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde. The party, in a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Abubakar Yusuf, on Friday, said Tinubu had failed to demonstrate what it described as the leadership required to address the country’s security and economic challenges. Yusuf alleged that the President had “abdicated his official duties” to family members, aides and other unelected persons. He also faulted Tinubu’s absence from the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, where Vice-President Kashim Shettima represented Nigeria and delivered the country’s national statement. The APM spokesman said the President’s absence from the gathering of world leaders reflected what the party described as his inability to effectively represent Nigeria’s interests at the international level. “Mr President’s repeated absence at meetings of world leaders, particularly the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), also underscores his inability to effectively represent, propagate and drive Nigeria’s interest at the global level where he was expected to engage in high-level diplomatic discussions on matters affecting our nation,” he said. Yusuf also criticised the administration’s handling of insecurity, alleging that Tinubu had neither visited communities affected by attacks nor directly met with victims and grieving families. “Is it not absurd that President Tinubu has never visited any of the communities being ravaged by terrorists, kidnappers and bandits? Is it not equally absurd that President Tinubu has never directly met with grieving families and victims?” he asked. He alleged that the administration’s response to insecurity had largely involved issuing statements, giving directives and sending delegations instead of direct visits to affected communities. Yusuf further claimed that more than 600,000 Nigerians had been killed by terrorist groups in the last three years. He did not provide supporting evidence for the figure in the statement. The APM also faulted the administration’s economic policies, particularly the removal of the petrol subsidy, tax reforms and external borrowing, which it said had worsened economic hardship and contributed to business closures. Yusuf cited Nigeria’s N159.28 trillion public debt, describing the figure as evidence of what he called reckless borrowing by the administration. The Debt Management Office had reported total public debt of N159.28 trillion as of December 31, 2025. Yusuf, however, alleged that there was little to show for the borrowed funds and claimed that some of the proceeds had been diverted to private interests. He did not provide evidence to support the allegation. He also claimed that more than 3.7 million Nigerian youths and professionals had left the country under the “Japa” phenomenon, describing the development as a major source of brain drain, particularly in the education and health sectors. The APM said Nigeria could not afford another four years under what it described as an “insensitive and rudderless administration.” “President Tinubu must understand that Nigeria requires a leader with full stamina, who is present, accessible and fully engaged in governance,” Yusuf said. He described Makinde as a “younger, energetic and experienced leader” with a record in Oyo State and said the governor had a blueprint to “reset Nigeria.” The APM therefore urged Tinubu to reconsider his bid for a second term, withdraw from the 2027 presidential race and support Makinde “in the overall interest of the nation.” The post APM asks Tinubu to quit 2027 race, back Makinde appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Yémen : les combats s’intensifient, les Houthis ciblent à nouveau Riyad (VIDEO)
items.description: La guerre au Yemen connaît sa plus forte escalade depuis la treve de 2022. Dans la nuit du 25 au 26 septembre, la coalition menee par l'Arabie saoudite a annonce avoir intercepte deux drones houthis lances vers Riyad, ainsi qu'un missile balistique visant Khamis Mushait, dans le sud-ouest du royaume. Un nouvel episode apres l'attaque du 19 septembre contre la capitale saoudienne et les salves du 24 septembre contre Taïf et Yanbu, principal debouche petrolier saoudien sur la mer Rouge. عاجل الآن🚨 هجوم يمني واسع على أهداف سعودية في الرياض وأبها وخميس مشيط وانفجارات عنيفة تهز السعودية pic.twitter.com/CHPyqQMfK1 — أخبار اليمن | Yemen News (@Yemen_News0) September 26, 2026 Sur le terrain, les combats se concentrent desormais autour de Taez et Lahj. Les Houthis, qui ont pris Mokha et renforce leur presence autour de Bab el-Mandeb, cherchent a progresser vers les hauteurs dominant le detroit. Les forces gouvernementales, appuyees par les Brigades des Geants, les Forces du Bouclier de la Patrie et des tribus locales, ont repris plusieurs positions montagneuses, dont le mont Nouman, afin d'empecher les Houthis de couper l'axe reliant Aden, Lahj et Taez au littoral occidental. 900 frappes saoudiennes Les frappes contre les positions houthies se poursuivent parallelement. Le mouvement affirme que plus de 900 frappes aeriennes et tirs de missiles ont vise ses positions depuis le debut de l'escalade, notamment a Mokha, Bab el-Mandeb, Taez, Saada et Marib, un chiffre qui semble impossible a verifier independamment. Riyad presente ses operations comme une reponse aux attaques contre son territoire et ses infrastructures. Le conflit deborde desormais largement du cadre yemenite. Les Houthis disposent d'un levier sur Bab el-Mandeb tout en frappant directement le territoire saoudien. Pour Riyad, l'enjeu est double : contenir leur avancee au Yemen et proteger ses villes, ses infrastructures petrolieres et ses routes d'exportation. Le coût humain s'alourdit : l'OMS recensait 674 morts et 2 998 blesses entre le 6 août et le 18 septembre, tandis que le HCR comptait plus de 130 000 nouveaux deplaces depuis debut septembre.

items.title: Nigeria has finished making sacrifices — Tinubu
items.description: By Gift Chapi Odekina, Abuja President Bola Tinubu has assured Nigerians that the country is on the right path, declaring that the nation has “finished making sacrifices” and that peace and development will return. Tinubu gave the assurance in a message delivered by the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rep. Tajudeen Abbas, at a special prayer session marking Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary at the National Mosque, Abuja, on Friday. Tajudeen, who represented the President at the event, urged Nigerians not to lose hope despite the challenges confronting the country, saying the sacrifices made over the years would ultimately yield a better Nigeria. “I want to categorically make it clear that Nigeria is on the right path. There is light at the end of the tunnel. Nigeria has finished making sacrifices for this country to be great again,” Tajudeen quoted the President as saying. The President acknowledged the difficulties Nigerians had experienced, but said the country’s 66 years of nationhood had also been characterised by growth, resilience and significant achievements. According to him, Nigeria had matured as a nation and must build on the lessons of its journey since independence. “Any person of 66 years cannot be called a child anymore. Nigeria has become mature, even though when we reflect on the journey from independence to date, Nigeria was bedevilled with a lot of issues in the past, and opportunities as well,” he said. Tajudeen said the President’s message was aimed at restoring confidence among Nigerians and encouraging citizens to remain committed to the country despite prevailing difficulties. “My message to the country on behalf of Mr President, the Senate President and all members of the National Assembly is that people should not lose hope. “Peace is coming back to this country, development is coming back to this country. Things will get better as we progress in this democracy,” he said. The Speaker said Nigeria’s democratic journey remained critical to addressing longstanding challenges, strengthening institutions and creating conditions for sustainable development. He urged Nigerians to give the government’s policies and programmes time to deliver, noting that some of the challenges confronting the country had accumulated over several years. Tajudeen also said the National Assembly would continue to support measures aimed at strengthening democracy, improving security, promoting economic development and enhancing the welfare of citizens. He stressed that nation-building could not be left to government alone, calling for greater unity and citizen participation in the development of the country. The Speaker urged Nigerians to use the anniversary to reflect on the nation’s journey, acknowledge its achievements and setbacks, and renew their commitment to building a peaceful, prosperous and united country. The prayer session was attended by dignitaries and Muslim faithful, who offered prayers for peace, stability and continued development in Nigeria. The post Nigeria has finished making sacrifices — Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: KC Luxury, two others face 22-count drug charges
items.description: LAGOS — The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has filed a 22-count charge against Afolabi Kazeem Michael, popularly known as KC Luxury, and two others over the alleged shipment of 184.5 kilogrammes of cocaine to London, United Kingdom. Afolabi was arraigned alongside Boniface Freeman Ochoche Sule and Ikechukwu Ekugo Patriarch before Justice Musa Kakaki of the Federal High Court in Lagos on Friday. The three defendants pleaded not guilty to charges bordering on cocaine trafficking, illegal export of narcotics and money laundering. The case, marked FHC/LAG/CR/755/2026, centres on allegations that the defendants conspired between July 28 and August 1, 2026, with Atandare Oladipupo Oluwarotimi and Latifat Yusuf, who the NDLEA said had been arrested in London, to export the cocaine in five consignments through a Lagos-based courier logistics company. In the first count, the NDLEA alleged that the defendants conspired to export the cocaine in consignments bearing five airway bill numbers and shipped under the name Yemi Ejide. The charge sheet states that the defendants allegedly conspired to export 184.5kg of cocaine contained in five consignments with airway bill numbers 2079998314, 8224082370, 2079973571, 7181131742 and 2211893902, with the shipper’s name listed as “Yemi Ejide.” The alleged offence was said to be contrary to and punishable under Section 14(b) of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency Act, Cap. N30, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004. Other counts accuse Sule of allegedly procuring Ekugo to facilitate the export, while Afolabi was accused of procuring a staff member of BOT Express Logistics on Lagos Island to process the consignments. Afolabi was also accused of unlawfully possessing the cocaine ahead of its intended export. The charge sheet further alleges that N13.2 million was transferred from an account belonging to Mallamawa Ventures with Zenith Bank to BOT Express Logistics as payment for the shipment. Sixteen of the counts relate to alleged money laundering. The NDLEA accused Afolabi of moving billions of naira through corporate and personal accounts linked to Mallamawa Ventures, Fateey Man Multi-Purpose Nig. Ltd, Patonifa Ltd, Ade-Lak Resources, Holmestas Global Services Limited and La Capital Enterprises. The agency further alleged that the funds were used, among other things, to acquire motor vehicles and landed properties in an attempt to conceal the alleged proceeds of illicit activities. Afolabi was also accused of failing to declare his assets to the agency as required by law. Following the defendants’ pleas, NDLEA prosecutor, Abu Ibrahim, opposed their bail applications and urged the court to remand them in custody, citing the gravity of the alleged offences. Justice Kakaki subsequently ordered that the defendants be remanded in an NDLEA facility and adjourned the case until October 4, 2026, for ruling on their bail applications. According to the NDLEA, Afolabi was arrested by its operatives on August 13 after he allegedly attempted to leave Nigeria on a business-class flight to Paris from the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos. The arrest followed the interception of the 184.5kg cocaine shipment, which the agency estimated to be worth about N39 billion. The NDLEA said a subsequent search of Afolabi and his Banana Island apartment led to the recovery of exotic vehicles, foreign currency and jewellery allegedly linked to proceeds of the illicit trade. The case was adjourned until October 4, 2026, for ruling on the bail applications. The post KC Luxury, two others face 22-count drug charges appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Scales of deception removed – Annoh-Dompreh attacks new cocoa price
items.description: Minority Chief Whip Frank Annoh-Dompreh has criticised the government’s new cocoa producer price, describing the GH¢2,650 per 64-kilogramme bag as a disappointment to farmers. His comments followed the Ghana Cocoa Board’s announcement of a new producer price of GH¢42,400 per tonne for the 2026/2027 cocoa season. The new price, which took effect on September 25, translates into GH¢2,650 per 64kg bag. It represents an increase of GH¢1,008 per tonne over the GH¢41,392 per tonne price that prevailed during the 2025/2026 season. Reacting to the announcement in a series of posts on X, the Nsawam-Adoagyiri MP took issue with the new figure. “Cocoa new farm gate price: GH¢2650!!. Now, the ‘scales’ of deception have been removed. This govt. will contend with us & our cocoa farmers once more!” He subsequently intensified his criticism of the government, writing: “The impunity of this government is wild & ugly!” The MP also extended his concerns beyond cocoa, arguing that farmers producing other major food crops were facing difficulties. “Farmers generally have come under ‘attack’ under this administration: Rice, Maize, Yam, & Cocoa!!!” His comments come as Ghana’s cocoa sector undergoes significant changes in pricing, financing and governance. For the 2025/2026 season, the producer price had initially been set at GH¢51,392 per tonne. That figure was later revised to GH¢41,392 per tonne, equivalent to GH¢2,587 per 64kg bag, amid a sharp decline in international cocoa prices and liquidity challenges in the sector. COCOBOD subsequently maintained the GH¢41,392 price for the 2026 light crop season. The new GH¢42,400 per tonne price therefore gives farmers an additional GH¢1,008 for every tonne sold compared with the previous rate. COCOBOD says the new price represents 71.18 per cent of the realised gross Free-On-Board value of cocoa. The pricing decision has been introduced under the newly enacted Ghana Cocoa Board Act, 2026, which guarantees cocoa farmers a minimum of 70 per cent of the realised gross FOB value. The law also introduces changes to the financing and governance of the cocoa sector. COCOBOD Chief Executive Officer Dr Randy Abbey said the new price followed consultations with key stakeholders, including the Ministry of Finance, cocoa farmers, licensed buying companies, hauliers and processors. The Board has also indicated that the producer price could be reviewed if market conditions and other relevant factors warrant an adjustment. Beyond pricing, COCOBOD says it will continue productivity programmes designed to reduce the production burden on farmers and improve yields. These include free fertiliser, free hybrid cocoa seedlings and the Cocoa Disease and Pest Control Programme. The Board has also announced the nationwide deployment of the Ghana Cocoa Traceability System as part of efforts to meet emerging international market requirements. The latest price announcement therefore sets the stage for another debate over farmer incomes, cocoa-sector financing and the broader sustainability of Ghana’s cocoa industry. For Annoh-Dompreh, however, the GH¢2,650 farm-gate price has become a fresh point of confrontation between the government and cocoa farmers.

items.title: Tinubu to Nigerians: I’m correcting mistakes of past administrations, give me more time
items.description: ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu has asked Nigerians to give his administration more opportunity to complete what he described as the “good work” it has started, saying his government is correcting the mistakes and missed opportunities of previous administrations. Tinubu made the appeal through the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Tajudeen Abbas, on Friday at a special prayer session held at the National Mosque, Abuja, as part of activities marking Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary. The President said peace and development were gradually returning to the country, urging Nigerians not to lose hope. According to him, Nigeria’s 66 years of independence represented a significant milestone, although the country’s journey had been characterised by both challenges and opportunities. “This anniversary—the 66th—by all accounts signifies Nigeria has come of age,” he said. “The person of 66 years cannot be called a child anymore. Nigeria has become mature, even though when we reflect on the journey from independence to date, we may say it was a mixed journey. “Nigeria was bedevilled with a lot of issues in the past and opportunities as well. But we thank Almighty Allah for granting us the life and the peace for us to witness this very historic event today.” Tinubu urged Nigerians to remain hopeful about the country’s future, saying peace and development would return as democracy continued to deepen. “My message to the country on behalf of Mr President, the Senate President and all members of the National Assembly is that the citizens should not lose hope. “Peace is coming back to this country. Development is coming back to this country. Things will get better as we progress in this democracy.” He said the administration was focused on addressing what he described as the cumulative mistakes and missed opportunities of previous governments. “More importantly, citizens should look at the focus of the government of today, that the mistakes of the past—the cumulative mistakes and the missed opportunities of the past—are being corrected in this particular administration,” he said. Tinubu also said Nigeria was on the right path and that citizens had made the sacrifices necessary for the country to become great again. “And I want to categorically make it clear that Nigeria is on the right path; that there is light at the end of the tunnel, and that Nigerians have finished making sacrifices for this country to be great again. “We should give this government more opportunity for it to come back and finish the good work.” The appeal comes ahead of the 2027 general elections, when Tinubu is seeking another term in office. The Federal Government has said the 66th Independence Anniversary is being marked with a series of activities, including religious services, a public lecture and a nationwide broadcast by the President on October 1. Senior government officials, including Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin, state governors, members of the National Assembly, ministers, Secretary to the Government of the Federation, George Akume, and military chiefs, attended the prayer session. items.title: OpenAI admits AI agents posted ChatGPT users’ images online in error
items.description: OpenAI acknowledged Friday that its artificial intelligence tools had posted images from ChatGPT users onto online sites without the company’s knowledge, the latest example of AI agents operating outside their bounds. The company also confirmed a New York Times report that its tools had accessed websites of US federal agencies, saying they retrieved only publicly available information. Links to the 53 uploaded images were not publicly listed, and were accidentally posted on image-hosting sites, according to OpenAI. Most have been removed with the help of the hosting providers involved, and removal of the remaining images is underway, the San Francisco-based tech giant said. “We’ve shared details on how AI agents in our research environment sent training and evaluation data to third-party services when they shouldn’t have,” the company said in an X post. Dissemination of the images was caused by AI agents — software build on artificial intelligence models and capable of acting autonomously. The images in question came from the accounts of users who had authorized the use of the data to improve OpenAI’s models. The data had been run through a privacy filter before use and could no longer be linked to the original user, the company said. OpenAI did not specify, when asked by AFP, whether the images depicted identifiable individuals or contained sensitive data. – Rogue AI agents – According to OpenAI, agents that it uses for its research transmitted the training data to external platforms. The incidents occurred before OpenAI strengthened the security protocols of its research environment in August following other rogue actions by AI agents. The company said it is scrutinizing the past activity of its AI agents, work that “will take months to complete.” “Most of the activity we’ve reviewed so far involved routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions. Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information,” an OpenAI spokesperson told AFP. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman acknowledged Friday on X that “we have not been as fast as we would have liked” in reviewing and disclosing the incidents. But he said it was important to “balance our desire for transparency” with assessing the massive volume of data to be analyzed. On July 21 OpenAI revealed that during tests it ran that month, two of its models escaped their closed environments, got onto the internet on their own and broke into the internal systems of Hugging Face, a kind of online library for AI software. The episode drew wide attention and fed worries that the biggest AI companies cannot keep their own models under control. Altman reiterated Friday that the Hugging Face hack “is still the most severe event we’ve seen.” That discovery was followed by revelations of several similar incidents at OpenAI and its rivals, such as Anthropic and Meta. On Wednesday in New York, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorized access to a government health portal in June, and the leader criticized the company for delaying its notification to the authorities. AFP The post OpenAI admits AI agents posted ChatGPT users’ images online in error appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Five days inside the contradictions of the United Nations
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: Only at the United Nations can a journalist walk through a corridor and suddenly find himself face to face with a prime minister, pause before a sculpture symbolising peace, read the words of a Persian poet written on a wall, and then rush outside to report on a protest against a war thousands of miles away. For five days, I lived inside that extraordinary contradiction while covering the high-level debate of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. The official high-level week brought heads of state and government from around the world to the UN headquarters between September 22 and 26. The first thing one begins to notice at the United Nations is the art. There are sculptures, statues and works donated by countries that seem to confront you at every turn. They are reminders of peace, humanity, war and the hope that nations can somehow learn to live together. Even before you enter the United Nations, the place begins to tell its story. As you approach the Secretariat Building, you encounter Barbara Hepworth’s Single Form, the large abstract bronze standing beside the circular pool. Donated by Jacob Blaustein, it rises quietly against the building, its simple, powerful shape inviting a visitor to pause before entering a place where the world’s conflicts are debated. Nearby stands St. George Slaying the Dragon, a sculpture presented to the United Nations by the Soviet Union. The familiar image of St. George defeating the dragon takes on a different meaning here, surrounded by the flags and institutions of an organisation created in the aftermath of war. And then there is Antun Augustinčić’s Peace Monument, the mounted figure holding a sword and an olive branch. The Yugoslav/Croatian sculptor had wanted its silhouette to be visible from the East River, so that the idea of peace could announce itself even before a visitor reached the building. Further along is Carl Fredrik Reuterswärd’s Non-Violence, the bronze revolver with its barrel tied into a knot, a gift from Luxembourg. Nearby, Evgeniy Vuchetich’s Let Us Beat Swords into Ploughshares shows a man transforming a sword into a tool for cultivating the earth. Taken together, these sculptures seem to form a kind of preface to the United Nations: the human figure, the struggle against violence, the rejection of weapons and the hope that instruments of destruction can be transformed into instruments of peace. And then you enter the building, where the symbols continue. On an entrance are the words of the great Persian poet Saadi, reminding us that human beings are parts of one body, created from the same essence — and that when one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace. And then, inside the building, you encounter the words of Saadi, the great Persian poet, written on a wall. His famous lines describe human beings as parts of one body, created from the same essence. When one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace. I kept returning to those words during these five days. Because almost everywhere I looked, I saw the world struggling with the very idea they express. Iran and the United States were at the centre of intense diplomatic activity. Gaza dominated conversations inside the building and protests outside it. The war in Ukraine continued to draw attention, while India and Pakistan brought their familiar confrontation to the international forum. The United Nations seemed to contain the whole contradiction of our age: an institution built on the idea that humanity can act together, confronted every day by evidence of how difficult that remains. Outside the gates, protesters gathered in large numbers as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived to address the UN General Assembly. Inside, delegations walked out during his speech. And there I was, moving between the demonstrations, the diplomatic meetings, the press conferences and the Assembly hall, doing what journalists do — watching, listening, asking questions and trying to understand what was happening behind the carefully prepared language of diplomacy. At one point, I actually bumped into Netanyahu. It was not a planned interview or a formal meeting. It was simply one of those extraordinary moments possible only at the United Nations, where presidents, prime ministers, diplomats, security officers, journalists and interpreters are constantly crossing one another’s paths. The security arrangements themselves became part of the story. During the US president’s stay in New York, security around the United Nations was extraordinarily tight. Motorcades moved through sealed streets, access was restricted and every movement of a major leader seemed choreographed. The arrival of leaders such as the Syrian and Turkish presidents added to the atmosphere. Then the intensity would ease. A major leader would leave, the barricades would move, the corridors would become less crowded, and suddenly the United Nations would feel almost ordinary again—until another motorcade arrived. That rhythm is something a television broadcast cannot quite capture. At the UN, diplomacy is not only what leaders say from the podium. It is also the waiting, the corridors, the security checks, the hurried whispers, the chance encounters and the small conversations between meetings. Pakistan’s diplomatic role was another important part of my coverage. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Assembly as Islamabad continued efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States. Shehbaz later said Pezeshkian regarded the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding as fully acceptable to Iran and was prepared to move it forward. That is the other side of covering the UN. You see confrontation, but you also see countries trying to create channels through which confrontation might be reduced. And sometimes the most memorable moments have nothing to do with the major powers. Only at the United Nations could I find myself in a photograph with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman of Bangladesh, Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua of Tonga and Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo of Samoa. Three leaders from three very different parts of the world, standing together in New York. Only at the United Nations. The photograph captures something that statistics cannot. The General Assembly has 193 member states, each represented with one vote. Yet the world represented inside that building is vastly more complicated than a list of countries and votes. Every delegation carries its own history. Every leader brings his country’s anxieties. Every journalist arrives carrying questions. And outside, the protesters carry their anger. For five days, I walked past the sculptures and statues, past the flags and security barriers, past presidents and prime ministers, past demonstrations and diplomatic receptions. And each time I saw Saadi’s words on the wall, they seemed to ask the same simple question: If we really are parts of one body, how can one part suffer while the rest remains at peace? The United Nations has no easy answer. Perhaps that is why the question is still written on its wall. And perhaps that is why, after five days of covering the world’s most powerful people, the image I carry with me is not of a speech or a motorcade. It is of people from Bangladesh, Tonga, Samoa and Pakistan standing together for a photograph. Only at the United Nations.

items.title: US, China buy time with trade truce as pressure builds
items.description: Washington and Beijing may have bought themselves breathing space with an extended trade truce, but analysts warn that time is running out for the world’s two biggest economies to resolve their strategic rivalry. President Donald Trump and Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping concluded a pomp-filled summit on Friday, with the US leader confirming they would meet twice more this year. But even as Trump and Xi “are making nice”, their countries “remain locked in a bitter competition over trade, tech, Taiwan, defence, rare earths and industrial policy”, said Daniel Russel of the Asia Society Policy Institute. Daniel Kritenbrink, a former US official now with The Asia Group consultancy, said there’s “no doubt that both leaders would like to see stability in the relationship, at least through the end of the year”. However, “you’d have to see further tangible outcomes for this truce to extend in the long run”. Some feel Beijing has “largely not lived up to the commitments it made” at earlier meetings, he added, noting many US officials “have articulated their profound frustration with the Chinese”. Xi and Trump agreed to a trade truce last year during a meeting in South Korea, after a bitter tit-for-tat fight that saw tariffs soar over 100 percent at one point. As part of the agreement, Beijing agreed to buy more US soybeans and other agriculture products, and to suspend rare earths restrictions for a year. The pact was originally due to expire in November but both sides agreed this week to extend it until January 10, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Short leash Trump’s top trade official Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that Washington views such extensions as “compliance periods”. “I think US officials would say China is doing just barely enough to maintain the agreement and no more,” Kritenbrink said. “That’s unsustainable over the long run,” he added. The brief extension “was the preferred position of the Americans,” Mary Lovely of the Peterson Institute for International Economics told AFP . She added that while Beijing would have preferred a longer rollover, the current situation points to Washington’s anxiety about the delivery of rare earth magnets and how officials “want to keep this on a short leash”. “It’s not clear anymore how much their threats of high tariffs actually move China,” she said. ‘Bitter competition’ For now, Greer said that both countries have made “progress” on other economic outcomes and expect to release more details on Monday. “We want to have some subset of goods that we can trade with the Chinese on a more preferential basis,” he said. He added that both sides have agreed on products that can be left aside in future trade disputes. Greer is set to host G20 trade ministers in Wisconsin next week, with US tariff threats and the issue of excess capacity — a key concern surrounding Chinese industry — expected to be discussed. Washington and Beijing have also agreed to set up some kind of notification system for artificial intelligence threats between the two countries, Bessent said. Peter Richardson of Counterpoint Research said the channel could be as simple as a hotline, but it will be tough to define what triggers it. “It is often very difficult to tell quickly whether an AI incident was state-directed, a rogue actor or an accident,” he said. “Given the rivalry we don’t expect this to lead to any comprehensive international framework for AI regulation, but it would be the first practical guardrail,” he added. Kritenbrink, for his part, said the summit has done “nothing to curb the competitive instincts of both sides on AI”. “I don’t think you’ll see any slowing down.”

items.title: Notre regard sur la tentative de coup d’État contre Bourguiba en 1962
items.description: Il est des épisodes de l’histoire nationale qui, parce qu’ils ont été immédiatement enfermés dans un récit officiel, cessent presque de faire l’objet d’une véritable enquête historique. La tentative de coup d’État de décembre 1962 contre Habib Bourguiba est de ceux-là. Abdelhamid Larguèche * L’affaire semblait depuis longtemps classée : un groupe de militaires et de civils, conduit par Lazhar Chraïti, aurait projeté d’assassiner le président de la République et de renverser le régime. L’échec du complot, les arrestations, le procès devant le tribunal militaire et les condamnations avaient fourni les éléments d’un récit devenu dominant. Le mérite premier du nouveau livre de Mohamed El May, ‘‘محاولة الانقلاب على بورقيبة: مؤامرة 1962’’ , publié en 2026, est précisément de rouvrir ce dossier à partir des documents judiciaires et des paroles des principaux protagonistes. Ce n’est pas seulement un nouveau récit de l’affaire. C’est une invitation à relire une séquence décisive de l’histoire de la Tunisie indépendante. Faire parler ceux qui avaient été condamnés L’apport le plus important du livre réside dans la publication d’un ensemble documentaire considérable : vingt-cinq interrogatoires de prévenus, quatre plaidoiries de la défense, les dernières déclarations des accusés et le jugement. Ce choix est historiquement précieux. Pendant longtemps, les condamnés de 1962 ont surtout existé dans la mémoire publique à travers les accusations portées contre eux et le récit politique qui accompagna le procès. El May restitue leurs propres paroles. Non pas pour les transformer automatiquement en vérité, encore moins pour les réhabiliter, mais pour permettre à l'historien et au lecteur de mesurer la diversité de leurs positions, de leurs motivations et de leurs itinéraires. C’est là toute la différence entre une histoire racontée à partir d’un verdict et une histoire qui revient aux sources du dossier. Les interrogatoires ne constituent évidemment pas une parole transparente. Un accusé interrogé par les enquêteurs peut chercher à minimiser son rôle, à en charger un autre, à protéger des proches ou à présenter son engagement sous un jour plus favorable. Mais cette limite ne diminue pas leur intérêt. Elle impose au contraire de les confronter entre eux et de les croiser avec la presse de l’époque, les archives et les autres témoignages. C’est cette confrontation qui fait naître l’histoire. L’un des effets les plus intéressants de la documentation réunie par Mohamed El May concerne la place de Lazhar Chraïti dans l’affaire. Le récit traditionnel avait fortement personnalisé la tentative autour de sa figure. Or les interrogatoires font apparaître un paysage plus complexe, dans lequel Omar Bembli semble jouer un rôle beaucoup plus important que ne le laissait entendre le récit traditionnel. Il faudrait cependant éviter de remplacer une simplification par une autre : passer du « complot de Chraïti » au « complot de Ben Bembli » ne ferait que déplacer le problème. Ce que les documents semblent plutôt révéler, c’est l’existence d’un milieu hétérogène dans lequel se rencontrent des militaires, d’anciens combattants de la lutte nationale, des civils et des hommes issus de sensibilités politiques différentes. La question historique devient alors plus intéressante : comment des trajectoires aussi différentes ont-elles pu converger, à la fin de 1962, autour de l’idée d’une action contre le pouvoir de Bourguiba ? Les frustrations de l’après-indépendance C’est probablement sur ce terrain que le livre ouvre les pistes les plus fécondes. Les témoignages réunis par El May font apparaître, derrière le projet politique, une accumulation de frustrations. Elles ne sont pas toutes de même nature. Il y a d’abord des griefs politiques : le règlement de la question de Bizerte, les rapports avec la France, les choix effectués après l’indépendance, la concentration progressive des pouvoirs et la place réservée aux différentes composantes du mouvement national. Mais il existe aussi une autre dimension, plus sociale et personnelle. Certains anciens combattants semblent avoir considéré que leur participation à la lutte nationale leur donnait des droits particuliers dans l’État nouvellement indépendant : responsabilités, postes, autorisations, terres, avantages ou reconnaissance. Cette dimension est essentielle pour comprendre les tensions de l’après-indépendance. La génération qui avait combattu pour l’indépendance ne partageait pas nécessairement la même conception de ce que devait être l’État indépendant. Pour les uns, l’indépendance devait ouvrir une nouvelle étape de construction institutionnelle. Pour d’autres, ceux qui avaient combattu dans les maquis pouvaient considérer qu’ils étaient les véritables fondateurs de cet État et qu’ils devaient donc en occuper les premières places. Le conflit n’était donc pas seulement un conflit entre des individus et un président. Il touchait à une question beaucoup plus profonde : à qui appartient la légitimité dans un État nouvellement indépendant ? Pour les uns, l’indépendance devait ouvrir une nouvelle étape de construction institutionnelle. Pour d’autres, ceux qui avaient combattu dans les maquis pouvaient considérer qu’ils étaient les véritables fondateurs de cet État et qu’ils devaient donc en occuper les premières places. Le conflit n’était donc pas seulement un conflit entre des individus et un président. Il touchait à une question beaucoup plus profonde : à qui appartient la légitimité dans un État nouvellement indépendant ? La question de Bizerte apparaît également comme un élément important de cette histoire. La bataille de Bizerte de 1961 avait constitué un moment majeur de la mobilisation nationale. Mais son issue et les accords qui suivirent avaient nourri, dans certains milieux, des interrogations et des frustrations. Il faut ici distinguer les faits des mémoires politiques qui se sont construites autour d’eux. Ce qui importe historiquement, c’est que Bizerte apparaît dans les témoignages comme l’un des éléments à travers lesquels certains protagonistes de 1962 exprimaient leur désaccord avec les orientations du pouvoir. L’événement n’était donc pas seulement une affaire de personnes. Il s’inscrivait dans les débats, les déceptions et les recompositions politiques de la Tunisie des premières années de l’indépendance. Le procès est lui aussi un objet d’histoire Il serait cependant incomplet de s’arrêter aux préparatifs du complot. Le procès militaire de 1963 constitue lui-même un objet historique majeur. Les interrogatoires, les plaidoiries, les dernières paroles des accusés et le jugement publiés par Mohamed El May permettent de revenir sur la manière dont la justice militaire a traité cette affaire. Là encore, il faut éviter les conclusions trop rapides. Un procès politique ou militaire ne peut être étudié seulement à travers son verdict. Il faut regarder les conditions de l’instruction, la défense, les catégories d’accusation, les peines prononcées et la manière dont l’affaire fut ensuite intégrée au récit national. Autrement dit, l’historien doit étudier à la fois ce qui s’est passé en 1962 et la manière dont la Tunisie officielle a raconté ce qui s’était passé. C’est probablement l’un des grands intérêts du livre de Mohamed El May. À cet égard, un discours prononcé par Bourguiba après la découverte de la conspiration constitue une source particulièrement révélatrice. Bourguiba y présente l’affaire comme une menace directe contre sa personne et contre l’existence même de l’État. Il insiste sur les projets d’assassinat et sur la volonté supposée des conspirateurs de provoquer le chaos. Mais son discours apporte également un éclairage involontairement précieux sur les ressorts du conflit. Il revient longuement sur les anciens combattants, sur ceux qui considèrent que leur participation à la lutte nationale leur confère des droits particuliers et sur les frustrations liées aux postes, aux privilèges ou aux avantages attendus. Il affirme au contraire un principe qui est au cœur de sa conception de l’État : l’indépendance ne peut signifier la remise du pouvoir à ceux qui ont combattu les armes à la main. Tous les citoyens doivent être égaux devant l’État. Cette partie du discours mérite d’être confrontée aux témoignages publiés par El May. Non parce que le discours présidentiel constituerait la clé permettant de résoudre l’affaire, mais parce qu’il montre comment Bourguiba lui-même interprétait le conflit. De la légitimité révolutionnaire à la légitimité de l’État C’est peut-être ici que se trouve le véritable enjeu historique de 1962. Les premières années de l’indépendance sont marquées par le passage d’une légitimité de la lutte nationale à une légitimité fondée sur l’État. Ce passage ne va pas de soi. Ceux qui avaient combattu dans la clandestinité, dans les maquis ou dans les réseaux politiques pouvaient considérer que leurs sacrifices leur donnaient une place particulière dans la nouvelle Tunisie. Bourguiba défendait une conception différente : une fois l’indépendance acquise, la légitimité ne devait plus appartenir aux combattants en tant que tels, mais aux institutions de l’État. Le conflit de 1962 peut ainsi être lu comme l’un des moments où s'affrontent deux conceptions de la légitimité nationale. L’une s’appuie sur le sacrifice et le combat passé ; l’autre sur la construction d’un État centralisé, organisé et durable. Cette opposition n’épuise évidemment pas l’affaire. Elle ne doit pas faire oublier les ambitions personnelles, les rivalités politiques, les sensibilités idéologiques et les frustrations sociales qui apparaissent dans les témoignages. Mais elle permet de replacer l’événement dans une histoire plus large de la construction de l’État tunisien. Il faut enfin saluer une précaution essentielle que devrait conserver toute lecture du livre : rouvrir un dossier n’équivaut pas à réhabiliter ceux qui furent condamnés. L’historien n’est ni procureur ni avocat. Son travail consiste à établir les faits, à confronter les versions, à mesurer les contradictions et à restituer aux acteurs leur complexité. Le livre de Mohamed El May rend possible ce travail parce qu’il redonne accès à des sources qui permettent de dépasser le récit simplifié d’une affaire définitivement close. Il ne répond pas à toutes les questions. Et c’est précisément ce qui fait sa valeur. Il invite à poursuivre l’enquête : dans les archives de l’État, dans la presse de 1962-1963, dans les archives militaires et judiciaires, dans les mémoires des familles et dans les témoignages ultérieurs des protagonistes. Une affaire qui mérite enfin de sortir de la légende Soixante-quatre ans après les événements, la tentative de 1962 mérite donc autre chose qu'une répétition du récit qui s’est imposé au lendemain du procès. Le livre de Mohamed El May ne détruit pas ce récit. Il le met à l’épreuve des documents. Et c’est déjà beaucoup. En faisant entendre les accusés, en faisant apparaître la diversité des trajectoires, en donnant à voir les motivations politiques et sociales qui traversaient la Tunisie de l’après-indépendance et en permettant de revenir sur le procès lui-même, il transforme une affaire longtemps réduite à une « conspiration » en objet d’histoire. C’est probablement là son apport essentiel. L’intérêt de 1962 n’est pas seulement de savoir qui voulait renverser Bourguiba. Il est de comprendre pourquoi, quinze ans à peine après le début de la lutte nationale, des hommes issus de cette même histoire en sont venus à envisager une rupture violente avec le pouvoir issu de l’indépendance. * Historien. In memoriam : Lazhar Chraïti, père, pardonne-nous ! L’article Notre regard sur la tentative de coup d’État contre Bourguiba en 1962 est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Mohamed Benchicou, la dernière page d’une plume libre
items.description: Alors que le monde de la culture et des arts n’a pas encore fini de rendre hommage à l’homme du cinéma et grand comédien Sid Ahmed Agoumi , voilà qu’une autre figure, et non des moindres, emblématique de la presse algérienne, tire sa révérence. Mohamed Benchicou , décédé jeudi à Paris à l’âge de 74 ans, reste, de l’avis de tous, comme l’un des journalistes les plus brillants de sa génération. Journaliste à la plume acérée, redoutable polémiste, doublé d’un homme de grande culture avec qui seuls pouvaient rivaliser un Djaad, un Ameyar ou encore Naït Mazi, tous partis, mais ayant fait un bout de chemin ensemble dans l’aventure d’El Moudjahid, Mohamed Benchicou laisse la presse orpheline, même si l’exil l’a longtemps éloigné du pays. Une presse dont la trajectoire n'est certainement pas celle dont il a rêvé. Il part sans avoir vu les causes pour lesquelles il s’est investi corps et âme s’accomplir. Décès de Mohamed Benchicou : l’hommage émouvant de Yasmina Khadra « Encore un talent qui s’éteint dans un monde en perdition. Encore une plume qu’aucun encrier ne saurait désaltérer. Que c’est triste de devoir rendre hommage à un autre enfant prodige que notre patrie a déshérité, lui qui s’est tellement battu pour elle, pour la liberté, la justice et la démocratie. Parfois, j’ai le sentiment de subir la perte des braves d’Algérie comme une damnation. En particulier lorsque cette perte emporte des talents que j’ai connus et admirés », a réagi le grand écrivain Yasmina Khadra. Natif de Khemis Miliana, cette ville au pied du Zaccar qu’il a magnifiée dans de nombreux poèmes et chroniques, dont celle qu’il avait consacrée au père de Djamel Bensmaïl, originaire de la même ville, Mohamed Benchicou a entamé sa carrière de journaliste armé de deux leviers qui feront sa réputation : le talent et l'engagement. D’El Moudjahid au Matin On raconte que, durant son passage à El Moudjahid, lui, homme de gauche convaincu, journaliste à la rubrique sportive, n’hésitait pas, dans ses reportages, à glisser des messages politiques. C’était l’époque du parti unique et l’opposition était traquée et étouffée. À la fin des années 1980, au lendemain de l’ouverture démocratique, il va voir son directeur, Naït Mazi, pour lui annoncer qu’il quitte El Moudjahid pour relancer Alger Républicain. Il raconte cet épisode dans l’hommage émouvant qu’il lui rend en 2016. Benchicou y raconte comment un grand talent comme Naït Mazi avait servi sous le parti unique, déchiré entre la fidélité à une certaine idée du journalisme et la contrainte de se conformer à l’orientation politique du moment. « J’étais, en effet, le premier rédacteur à quitter ce journal où nous avions autant connu la richesse du métier que l’art de l’appauvrir », écrivait Benchicou. L’aventure d’Alger Républicain ne dura finalement pas, puisqu’il met la clé sous le paillasson au bout de quelques numéros. En 1991, il décide de se lancer dans une nouvelle aventure avec Saïd Mekbel en créant Le Matin. Très vite, le journal s’impose dans l’échiquier médiatique et devient l’un des titres les plus florissants de la presse nationale. Tout le monde garde en mémoire aujourd’hui les chroniques de « Aami Moh », en dernière page les week-ends, ou encore les « Unes » du journal, notamment lorsque Le Matin était en guerre contre le conseiller de Zeroual, Mohamed Betchine. À l’avènement de Bouteflika, Benchicou était l’un des rares à sonner la contestation, en révélant notamment les dessous de l’arrivée de certains hommes d’affaires des monarchies du Golfe, notamment des Émirats arabes unis, en Algérie. Son journal joue aussi un rôle de premier plan dans la couverture des événements qui ont secoué la Kabylie en 2001. Dans certains villages, Le Matin s’écoulait à 300 DA. Mais Benchicou n’était pas seulement un journaliste rigoureux. Il était aussi poète et écrivain. La descente aux enfers C’est la publication de son livre « Bouteflika, une imposture algérienne » qui lui causera des déboires et entamera sa descente aux enfers. Le livre met Benchicou dans le collimateur des autorités, notamment du défunt Yazid Zerhouni, qu’il avait tourné en ridicule dans sa gestion du « Printemps noir » et qui avait juré de le punir. Arrêté à l’aéroport en 2003 en possession de bons de caisse, il sera condamné en 2004 à deux ans de prison. Il sera libéré le 14 juin 2006 après avoir purgé sa peine à la prison d’El Harrach. Cette incarcération va le marquer profondément et lui laisser de nombreuses séquelles, notamment sur sa santé. De cette expérience carcérale, il tirera notamment « Les Geôles d’Alger » et « Journal d’un homme libre », deux ouvrages dans lesquels il reviendra sur la rudesse de l’enfermement et sur cette épreuve qui aura profondément marqué sa vie. Durant toute son incarcération, il jouira d’une grande solidarité internationale. Des journalistes du monde entier se mobilisent alors pour demander sa libération et, le 29 mars 2006, il reçoit le prix PEN qui rend hommage aux journalistes emprisonnés pour avoir exercé leur droit à la liberté d’expression. Pendant son incarcération, Le Matin est fermé. Mais, au niveau local, peu s’empressaient de le soutenir. Cette situation l’a beaucoup marqué. Et c’est naturellement qu’après sa sortie de quelques mois, il décide de s’installer en France. Même s’il a continué à diffuser son journal sur le Web, Benchicou, sans doute à la fois par l’exil, mais aussi par la désillusion, intervenait de moins en moins. Comme d’autres, il se manifestait à travers les réseaux sociaux, où il publiait de temps à autre, notamment durant le Hirak, dont il avait nourri le rêve et l'espoir de connaître une bonne issue. « Une plume au vitriol » Écrivain et journaliste, Arezki Metref résume ainsi l’homme et le journaliste : « Une plume au vitriol, un analyste redoutable et un homme d’une combativité sans concession qui aura payé le prix ultime pour son attachement viscéral à la liberté d’expression. Mohamed Benchicou, figure incontournable de la presse algérienne, incarnait l’alliance rare d’une vaste culture générale, d’une grande rigueur professionnelle et d’un engagement politique sans faille ». Metref rappelle également son parcours, d’El Moudjahid à Alger Républicain, puis au Matin, dont Benchicou était devenu la voix emblématique et le directeur courageux. Il souligne surtout que réduire Benchicou à la figure du polémiste redouté ou du directeur de journal engagé serait oublier l’écrivain, auteur d’une œuvre prolifique allant du témoignage carcéral à la fiction et aux biographies romancées. « Avec sa disparition, c’est toute une génération de journalistes, de lecteurs et de citoyens qui mesure l’ampleur de cette perte », dit-il. « Mohamed était un seigneur, un grand journaliste qui savait ciseler les mots, les dompter. Un grand liseur devant l’Éternel », souligne, pour sa part, le journaliste, critique d'art et universitaire, Ahmed Cheniki. « Mohamed Benchicou a été, est et restera cette plume magnifique, claire et fraîche comme l’eau d’une source, une plume qui osait traquer l’indicible, provoquer la vérité et interroger nos propres silences, une plume qui nous manquera assurément », souligne encore Yasmina Khadra. Avec sa disparition, c’est sans aucun doute une certaine idée du journalisme qui s’en va. C’est une page de la glorieuse aventure de la presse indépendante et de l’aventure intellectuelle qui se tourne. Mohamed Benchicou sera rapatrié ce samedi et sera enterré au cimetière de Garidi sur les hauteurs d’Alger. L’article Mohamed Benchicou, la dernière page d’une plume libre est apparu en premier sur TSA .
