items.title: Egypt’s Warning to Israel
items.description: W hen Israel’s leaders gathered in Jerusalem on September 26, 2023, to mark the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described the surprise assault by Syria and Egypt as a cautionary tale, one of missed intelligence warnings and self-delusion. “We do not underestimate any threat,” he said. Roughly two hours before Netanyahu took the stage, a chartered Cessna jet linked to Egypt’s intelligence service had touched down at Ben Gurion Airport, about 30 miles away. The jet rolled to a stop in an isolated section of the airport used for sensitive diplomatic and security missions. Abbas Kamel, Egypt’s intelligence chief and one of the region’s most influential security officials, had come to Israel on a most sensitive mission. Hamas, the Muslim Brotherhood–aligned terrorist group that controlled Gaza, appeared to be mobilizing for a major attack, Kamel said, according to Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, U.S., and European officials who were briefed about his visit after October 7. The window to prevent a disaster was closing. He recommended that the Israeli government grant Hamas economic concessions to avert conflict. His message, according to one former Israeli official later briefed on the visit, was: If you don’t change course, Gaza is going to blow up in your faces. Kamel didn’t provide Israeli officials with a date or specific information on what turned out to be a multipronged attack on Israel less than two weeks later, on October 7. And it’s not clear exactly with whom he met. The Egyptian plane remained on the ground in Israel for 67 minutes, according to an Israeli-airport-authority flight log, before returning to Cairo. (Independent flight-tracking applications confirm the plane’s journey.) What the Israeli officials did with Kamel’s warning remains an open question three years after the most devastating surprise attack in Israel’s history. But officials from seven different countries I spoke with said that Kamel’s visit should have set off alarms across the top ranks of the Israeli government. Netanyahu attended a classified briefing following the Yom Kippur War commemoration, according to his public schedule, and soon after approved some economic concessions to Hamas. Officials who spoke with me stressed that the mere presence of the Egyptian intelligence chief in Israel should have demonstrated the urgency of the issue. “The messenger was the message,” a former Israeli official told me. “There is no world,” this official said, where top Israeli officials meet with the head of Egyptian intelligence “and Bibi is not aware.” Netanyahu’s office, in the days after the attack, denied that he’d received any warnings, directly or indirectly, from Egypt over the situation in Gaza. Spokesmen for Netanyahu and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi didn’t respond to my repeated requests for comment when I asked about Kamel’s visit. The then-head of Netanyahu’s national-security council, Tzachi Hanegbi, denied to me this week that there had been a visit from Kamel or an Egyptian warning of any kind. Kamel’s 2023 visit, details of which have not been previously reported, underscores what dozens of sources have told me: that the Israeli government was repeatedly told of threatening activity by Hamas in the lead-up to October 7. A United Nations envoy who was in the Middle East at the time publicly warned of a latent conflict that could bring “grave consequences” while privately scrambling to defuse tensions between Israel and Hamas. The president of the United Arab Emirates, Mohamed bin Zayed, called Netanyahu to warn about the possibility of an imminent attack, after being briefed on intelligence findings from Egyptian and Palestinian sources, according to U.S. and Arab officials with knowledge of the call. Earlier this month, Israel’s Haaretz reported the leaders’ call; I confirmed with multiple officials that the call took place. Netanyahu denied the report and has threatened to sue Haaretz . The UAE didn’t respond to a request for comment. [ Read: Netanyahu just admitted he’s unfit to lead Israel ] Current and former Israeli, Arab, and U.S. officials tell me that they all experienced the same phenomenon in 2023: an arrogance on the part of Netanyahu bred by the deep-seated belief that Israel had the upper hand against Hamas. “It seemed clear that, for whatever reason, the West Bank was their priority,” a former senior U.S. official involved in talks with the Israeli government told me. “They were confident—even cocky—that they had the situation under control.” The Hamas attack, 11 days after Kamel’s visit, resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,200 people, primarily civilians, and the abduction into Gaza of 251 hostages during coordinated raids on communities, military bases, and an outdoor music festival. Israel launched a crushing retaliatory campaign that killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza, the majority of whom were civilians, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Hamas’s leadership and thousands of combatants have been killed. The attacks on Israel and the Gaza war that followed produced one of the more devastating humanitarian tragedies of the 21st century. The Netanyahu government’s stunning lack of preparation before the October 7 invasion is perhaps the most important issue in next month’s Israeli election. Netanyahu, who has been prime minister longer than any other politician in Israel’s history, is facing the most serious challenge of his career. Many Israelis, including Netanyahu’s main rival, the former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, have demanded an independent state inquiry into the military and intelligence failures in the run-up to the October 7 attacks. But Netanyahu has continuously refused to set up the kind of independent inquiry that followed past security failures, including the Yom Kippur War. The prime minister has instead attempted to establish a politically appointed commission of inquiry, which he said would include opposition representatives. The attempt was highly controversial; opposition leaders have refused to advance the proposal over concerns that the probe would favor Netanyahu’s government. While the wait for an inquiry continues, dozens of current and former Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, European, and U.S. officials have spoken with me, and their accounts help tell the story of what went wrong that fall. S ince Egypt and Israel signed the Camp David peace accords, in 1978, their relationship can be described as, at best, a cold peace. But the two nations have a common desire to subdue the threat of Hamas and other militant groups in Gaza, which borders both countries. Intelligence sharing between Egypt and Israel has thrived, particularly since al-Sisi became president, in 2014—even when their diplomatic relationship founders. Most of the intelligence reports in the weeks before the October 7 attacks, including Egypt’s, pointed to the renewal of conventional attacks—such as rocket fire—by Hamas and other armed factions in Gaza. They also warned of a spillover of violence into the West Bank. But intelligence sources inside Gaza conveyed to Egypt a more ominous picture, leading Egypt and the UAE to flag to Israel the prospect that something unprecedented was in the works. “For Kamel to go to Israel” for a single hour, an Egyptian official told me about the September 2023 visit, “meant that al-Sisi himself felt: You need to go there and tell them yourself .” The Israeli government’s focus, however, was elsewhere. The country was already in the grip of its deepest domestic crisis in decades. For months, Israel had been consumed by Netanyahu’s effort to overhaul the judicial system, a constitutional confrontation that was protested by hundreds of thousands and opened deep fissures within the military and within society. And a surge in Israeli-Palestinian violence in the West Bank had already made 2023 the deadliest year in decades for West Bank Palestinians, with Israeli military raids, Palestinian attacks, and settler violence contributing to the combustible atmosphere. Israel surged military personnel and resources into the territory. Biden-administration officials sought to ease tensions in the West Bank while other international and regional negotiators focused on Gaza. [ Read: Israel can’t postpone its reckoning forever ] Israel established a comprehensive land, sea, and air blockade of Gaza in 2007, when Hamas seized control of the territory, and crossings at Egypt’s border with Gaza, in Rafah, have been tightly restricted since. Freedom of movement became virtually impossible for the 2.1 million people who lived in the 141-square-mile territory. Israel and Hamas had last fought a war there in May 2021. That 11-day conflict ended in a cease-fire—brokered, notably, by Kamel, among others. Hamas appeared to have little interest in abandoning the uneasy truce. But international observers picked up on signs that the situation inside Gaza was changing. Long before the summer of 2023, one international negotiator in the region told me, contacts were reporting that “something was cooking,” though the details were vague and the signals confusing. By August, tensions in Gaza had clearly heightened, in part because Qatar froze deliveries of Egyptian fuel that it had been sending to Gaza since 2021. Hamas resold the fuel and used the proceeds to help pay public-sector workers, a key mechanism by which it maintained control in the Strip. Hamas called for demonstrations at the Erez border crossing over Qatar’s delayed aid, as well as other lingering disputes like the treatment of Palestinian prisoners. The crossing is the primary pedestrian gateway between Israel and Gaza and an especially important one for Gazan workers. Israel responded to the protests in mid-September by closing the crossing. Roughly 18,000 Gazans had permits to work in Israel. After those people were barred from going to work, “the escalation started to come much faster,” one negotiator told me. The Arabic outlet Rai al-Youm , citing Palestinian sources, reported on September 26 that Hamas had conveyed to the Egyptian government that Gaza would explode over the Erez closure. That same day, Kamel’s plane flew to Israel. Negotiators from Egypt, Qatar, and the United Nations scrambled to maintain calm. Hamas officials responded with what one international negotiator described as a broad “shopping list” of demands, including more permits to work inside Israel and the restoration of the fuel-for-public-salaries arrangement with Qatar. After the talks concluded in the final days of September, Hamas agreed to pull people back from the border fence and to try to ease tensions. Israel agreed to reopen the Erez crossing and to restore a medical-supply line into Gaza, adding that it would consider increasing the number of work permits. Still, the situation remained turbulent. On September 27, 10 days before the attack, Tor Wennesland, the UN’s special coordinator for the Middle East peace process, left Gaza with a stark warning: “The situation inside the Strip is dire and we must avoid another conflict that will have grave consequences for all,” Wennesland wrote on X. A day later, the new arrangement appeared to be taking hold. European diplomats who visited Erez watched as Gazan workers streamed back into Israel. But negotiators told me it later became clear that Hamas was using the talks as a ploy to buy time while finalizing its attack plans. Documents recovered by Israel from Gaza revealed that Hamas regarded the 2021 conflict as a triumph, and in its aftermath began planning for a breathtakingly large operation. A detailed memorandum from August 2022, apparently handwritten by Yahya Sinwar, then the leader of Hamas in Gaza, laid out much of the operational plan that the group would put into effect the following year. Even as international mediators focused on issues such as work permits and fuel deliveries, believing that these could defuse tensions, Hamas continued its relentless preparations for a massive attack. U.S. and Israeli military analysts told me Israel misinterpreted Hamas’s intentions, concluding that the group had no desire for military confrontation. K amel’s visits to Israel are rare. His last known trips were in May and August 2021, following that year’s Israel-Hamas war. After Kamel’s September 2023 trip, Egypt continued to raise the alarm up until two days before the attack, according to U.S., Egyptian, and Israeli officials with direct knowledge of those communications. American and Israeli officials told me it is unclear whether Kamel’s message could have been understood as foretelling the unprecedented attack that followed. Most of the warnings that Israel received in 2023 contained no date, target, or method of attack. But they were frequent and persistent. Around the same time, Netanyahu received the call from bin Zayed, whose country had normalized relations with Israel only three years earlier. In the call, bin Zayed reportedly sought to convey his assessment that Sinwar was planning a major attack. Like Kamel, bin Zayed urged Netanyahu to make economic concessions to Gaza. But Netanyahu seemed unmoved, two Arab officials familiar with the call told me. UN negotiators, U.S. officials, and international groups sensed that tensions in Gaza were exceptionally high, but told me they hadn’t been aware of any particular plans for an attack. On September 28, the CIA issued an internal report about a possible Hamas escalation in Gaza, reportedly based in part on foreign intelligence services. U.S. officials told me that report described the possibility that Hamas would launch rockets into Israel over several days. A second report, dated October 5, built on the first but was more analytical than revelatory. Neither detected rehearsals for a coordinated, multipronged attack like the one Hamas carried out two days later. On October 5, a message from Egypt to Israel also reiterated concerns that the situation was untenable, U.S., Egyptian and Israeli officials said. It provided no date or methodology, but conveyed urgency about a possible attack, the officials said. Egypt also shared its assessments with several other nations in the region, including Saudi Arabia, a senior Gulf Arab official told me. Jordan’s intelligence chief also conveyed concerns to his Israeli counterparts, according to Arab officials, that the situation had grown potentially explosive, especially in the West Bank, and needed to be addressed swiftly. (Spokespeople for Jordan’s government and intelligence service didn’t respond to a request for comment.) Biden-administration officials told me that neither Egypt nor the UAE shared such warnings with them ahead of October 7. U.S., Egyptian, Arab, and Israeli officials gave me a range of reasons why. Several people told me the warnings were too vague to warrant sharing with the U.S. Other officials, including those from the region, told me it was up to Netanyahu’s government to share the findings with Washington. (U.S. officials I spoke with dismissed this explanation, suggesting that if Egypt or Abu Dhabi had a pressing warning for Israel, Washington should have heard about it from them.) Several months after the attack, CIA Director William Burns was told, almost in passing, about both Kamel’s visit to Israel and bin Zayed’s call, but was not told about the specifics of their outreach, according to U.S., Israeli, and Arab officials. [ Read: Netanyahu doesn’t want the truth to come out ] Two days after the attack, as Israel took stock of the tragedy and its military campaign in Gaza began, Netanyahu’s office rejected press reports that he’d received any outreach from Kamel or Egypt. “The Prime Minister has neither spoken, nor met, with the head of Egyptian intelligence since the formation of the government, neither directly nor indirectly,” his office said on X . But the distinction between direct contact and intelligence passed through aides and other officials would become central to the debate over whether Israel could have done more to anticipate the attacks. On October 11, then–House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Michael McCaul told reporters after a classified briefing for lawmakers that Egypt had warned Israel. “We know that Egypt had warned the Israelis three days prior that an event like this could happen,” McCaul said. “I don’t want to get too much into classified, but a warning was given. I think the question was at what level.” (McCaul didn’t respond to my repeated attempts to discuss his comments.) In the months that followed, Israeli officials described a broader failure to interpret the signals coming from Gaza. In leaked recordings of briefings to bereaved families and residents obtained by Israel’s Channel 12, Herzi Halevi, then the chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, described the military establishment as having been “ lulled to sleep .” In a separate leaked recording , Halevi told local council chiefs that before the attacks, he had regarded Gaza “as the last border that needed attention.” Halevi resigned from his position in March 2025, and that June, the head of the Israel Security Agency, Ronen Bar, resigned under pressure over intelligence failures linked to the October 7 attacks. Hanegbi, the head of Netanyahu’s security council, was replaced in October 2025. Kamel, who left Egypt’s General Intelligence Service in October 2024, is now an adviser and special envoy for al-Sisi. S ince the October 7 attacks , Israel not only launched a crushing retaliation in Gaza, but later opened military fronts against Lebanon’s Hezbollah and, this year, a war in Iran. It’s impossible to know what would have happened if the warnings from Kamel and others had been heeded at the time, but it’s hard to imagine that Israel wouldn’t have been better prepared. As it was, the attacks caught the Israeli security services flat-footed. Reserve forces weren’t immediately available after kibbutz communities were attacked, leaving them defended primarily by local, lightly armed civilian volunteer forces from about 6:30 a.m., when the attacks began, to 1:30 p.m., when significant IDF reinforcements arrived. Netanyahu said in a campaign video clip last month that Israeli security officials failed to immediately wake him on the morning of October 7. “In the lead-up to October, there were so many warning signs, so many indications, that an attack was imminent,” Netanyahu said, without offering any specifics. “Had they woken me up, everything would have looked different. That is the story of October 7th—that is the story.” Today, Gaza remains in ruins and violence continues, despite efforts by the Biden and Trump administrations to secure a cease-fire. An April assessment by the UN, the World Bank, and the European Union estimated that $71.4 billion would be needed over the next decade for Gaza’s recovery and reconstruction. The great majority of its population remains displaced. Meanwhile, the trauma of October 7 lives on for Israelis. And bereaved families from that day continue to search for answers about how Hamas was able to engage in a devastating attack on Israel that appeared to catch the government completely by surprise. Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed reporting to this story. * Illustration sources: Getty; Khaled Desouki / AFP / Getty; Anadolu / Getty; Fatih Aktas / Anadolu / Getty

items.title: The Show That Always Chased Ratings, No Matter the Cost
items.description: To Catch a Predator may have presented a simulation of reality, but it was just convincing enough for viewers. The show’s objective was to apprehend people suspected of child sex abuse—which it did by staging sting operations. Its host, Chris Hansen, and his collaborators at Dateline NBC would sparsely furnish the entryway of some rented suburban home; an adult actor posing as a teenager would open the door for a stranger he or she had been chatting with online; and Hansen, who worked as a Dateline correspondent, would lurk in another room, waiting for the right moment to present himself to the houseguest and laconically intervene. His catchphrase was “Have a seat,” which he would utter while inviting his latest subject to take stock of the nightmare unfolding around him: He was suspected of intending to have sex with a minor, Hansen would explain, and now they were on candid camera—the police waiting just outside. Hansen’s somewhat maniacal pursuit of what he considered justice was detailed in last year’s very solid documentary Predators , which explored the legal and ethical limits of To Catch a Predator ’s blockbuster public-shaming approach. The new movie Primetime , a fictionalized look at the host’s meteoric rise and sudden implosion, also has a critical edge, but it’s much more interested in the weird version of real life that Hansen’s show created. The drama, from the director Lance Oppenheim, plunges the viewer into a sordid vision of early-2000s news entertainment—flashy, shallow, flimsy. And it revolves around an energetic Robert Pattinson performance that always feels a little sweaty and desperate to please the audience. Primetime is a beautiful nightmare—and might feel seductive to anyone who wanted to work in the world of gaudy TV journalism in 2004. That’s when the first To Catch a Predator segment premiered on NBC. It was followed by another, in 2005, before airing as a more regular series from 2006 to 2007. When the program ended, it did so amid a legal accusation of wrongdoing (the case was settled) and questions about its ethics. But during the years it ran, popular culture portrayed Hansen as a righteous crusader. His method—ensnaring alleged sex offenders in online traps meant to expose their dark proclivities, before turning them over to law enforcement—made for satisfying TV, mixing the trashiness of Jerry Springer –style talk shows with the aesthetics of supposed hard-news journalism. [ Read: Jerry Springer explained it all ] Casting Pattinson, a true movie star, as Hansen should stack the deck in the character’s favor: He dazzles on-screen. The actor has long been drawn to playing nervy oddities or handsome devils with some insecurity simmering beneath the surface. He portrays Hansen as sharklike and occasionally charming, unable to drop the facade he’s created for his show. His smirk is frozen, his voice affected. He seems to be constantly preening for cameras that aren’t always there. Pattinson’s performance comes across as fake in just the right ways—it’s an impersonation of someone who was himself living as an impersonator. Oppenheim primarily works as a documentarian, and has long been drawn to the anonymous-feeling tract housing and chintzy suburbs that To Catch a Predator made its domain. His documentary Some Kind of Heaven was about a group of retirees living in The Villages, a master-planned neighborhood for senior citizens; Spermworld explored the unregulated online marketplaces for sperm donation, for which people meet in motels to arrange DIY insemination. In Primetime , the director’s first narrative feature, the Dateline crew infiltrate similar types of communities to wreak gleeful havoc in the name of ratings. But the movie doesn’t condemn their efforts so much as it tries to understand how Hansen’s thirst for success infected everyone around him. (The real Hansen has criticized the film, declaring it “detached from reality.”) The most captivating storyline, in fact, is that of a decoy performer. The aspiring Hollywood actor Dan Plumb (played by Skyler Gisondo) takes the gig because he wants a union card, then quickly finds himself dangled in front of suspected sexual predators with little warning. Gisondo’s performance is as sweet and guileless as Pattinson’s is intense and unsettling; Dan has mighty career ambitions, but he sadly fails to grow beyond his seemingly eternal youth and the specific role Hansen has cast him in. Caught between them is the show’s producer Andie (the incredible Merritt Wever), who suppresses any qualms about her professional ethics in search of the show’s next target. Oppenheim imagines the tale of To Catch a Predator as a story of America. This is apt, considering how many stories about this country involve people pursuing success at any cost—one that typically ends up being very high. Primetime eventually careers toward disaster (drawn from the real-life incident that ended the show’s run), but any viewer can see that coming. More fascinating to behold is Hansen’s delight as he gets closer and closer to that grand catastrophe.

items.title: Health Ministry moves to integrate traditional medicine into mainstream healthcare
items.description: The Deputy Minister for Health, Prof. Dr Grace Ayensu-Danquah, has called for greater integration of scientifically validated traditional medicine into Ghana’s mainstream healthcare system. She said traditional medicine, when properly researched, regulated and manufactured to approved standards, could play a significant role in expanding access to safe and quality healthcare. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah made the call when she visited the Centre of Awareness (COA) Research and Manufacturing Company in the Central Region, where she engaged management and staff and inspected the company’s facilities to assess its compliance with Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP). She said Ghana could learn from countries such as China, where traditional and conventional medicine are used alongside each other to complement healthcare delivery. According to her, closer collaboration between the two sectors could help improve healthcare outcomes while ensuring that traditional medicines used by the public meet the required standards for safety, quality and effectiveness. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah said the government’s Free Primary Healthcare programme, which places emphasis on preventive and promotive healthcare, also presented an opportunity to examine how traditional medicine could contribute to the delivery of primary healthcare. She identified non-communicable diseases, including hypertension and diabetes, as areas where traditional medicine could potentially contribute, subject to scientific validation and appropriate regulation. The CEO of COA Manufacturing Company, Prof. (HC) Samuel Ato Duncan, welcomed the government’s efforts to develop the traditional medicine sector to a standard that would enable it to complement national healthcare programmes, including the Free Primary Healthcare initiative. He said the company was undertaking research into the potential health benefits of some of its products, including their possible applications in the management of cancer and viral diseases. Prof. Duncan stressed the importance of continued research and collaboration between traditional medicine practitioners, researchers and government institutions in unlocking the potential of the sector. He said such collaboration could help strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicines and enable the sector to make a greater contribution to healthcare delivery in Ghana. Prof. Ayensu-Danquah said the Ministry of Health would continue to work with relevant stakeholders to strengthen research, quality assurance, manufacturing and regulation within the traditional medicine sector. She said the broader objective was to create a healthcare system in which traditional and conventional medicine could complement each other safely, based on scientific evidence and appropriate regulatory standards.

items.title: 550 pupils in Kintampo South get educational lifeline as ‘Seeds of Hope’ reaches farming communities
items.description: More than 550 pupils in two farming communities in the Kintampo South District have received school supplies as part of an outreach programme aimed at easing some of the educational challenges confronting children in rural Ghana. The intervention formed part of the 2026 “Seeds of Hope” Community Outreach and School Donation Campaign by SeedSpark Foundation, in partnership with Legacy Impact through the Legacy Career Institute and OhenebaCare Foundation. The school gates in Anokyekrom and Abom Komkomba had barely opened on Monday, September 21, 2026, when the communities began buzzing with activity. Volunteers were setting up, health workers were preparing for free screening, and boxes of books and other educational materials were being arranged for pupils. For the children, however, the excitement was about more than a change from the usual school routine. They were about to receive some of the basic items many of them need to participate fully in the classroom. A total of 250 pupils in Anokyekrom and 300 in Abom Komkomba, from Kindergarten through Junior High School, received exercise books, textbooks, pens, pencils, rulers, school bags, clothing and footballs. The schools also received textbooks and Teaching and Learning Materials for use by teachers. For some teachers, the donation addresses a challenge that is familiar in many rural classrooms — trying to deliver lessons with limited teaching and learning resources. A teacher at Abom Komkomba D/A School welcomed the intervention, saying the textbooks would support both teachers and pupils. “The textbooks we’ve received will help us study and teach the kids,” she said. She added that some pupils regularly report to school without exercise books, making the donation particularly important. “This will help them and make learning and teaching enjoyable and easier. God bless SeedSpark Foundation,” she said. Executive Director of SeedSpark Foundation, Henry Ekow Yawson, said the organisation deliberately focuses on farming communities, where children can sometimes have fewer educational resources despite their communities playing an important role in Ghana’s food production. “Communities like Anokyekrom and Abom Komkomba are the backbone of this country’s food supply, yet their children are often the last to receive the tools they need to learn,” he said. According to him, the Foundation intends to continue returning to such communities because educational opportunity should not depend on where a child is born. “Every child deserves a fair shot, no matter where they’re born,” he added. The organisers say the intervention was designed to go beyond a one-day distribution exercise. Director of Legacy Impact, David, spoke to the pupils about opportunities available through the Legacy Career Institute and encouraged them to remain committed to their education. He said the objective was to help the children understand that their current circumstances do not have to define the limits of their future. “We don’t just want to hand out books and leave. We want these children to know that there’s a path beyond this classroom,” he said. Volunteers also spent time with the pupils, engaging them through games, singing and conversations. For the organisers, those interactions were just as important as the physical donations because they created an opportunity to encourage the children directly. The outreach also brought healthcare services closer to residents. An 18-member medical team comprising personnel from Kintampo South Hospital, OhenebaCare Foundation and the National Health Insurance Scheme screened an estimated 160 residents. The NHIS component was particularly targeted at helping residents understand and access the scheme while ensuring farmers who needed registration or renewal support could receive it during the outreach. Organisers plan to expand the campaign to more communities and undertake follow-up visits. Those visits are expected to help identify and respond to some of the needs uncovered during the education and health activities. By the end of the day, the classrooms at Anokyekrom and Abom Komkomba had gained new teaching materials, hundreds of pupils had received school supplies and dozens of residents had accessed health services. But for SeedSpark Foundation and its partners, the campaign represents something broader than a single day’s activities. It is an attempt to put practical resources behind a simple proposition: that a child’s access to education should not be determined by whether they grow up in a farming community or a major urban centre. The Foundation says the work will continue under its guiding motto: “Seeds of Change, Sprout of Success.”

items.title: Dr Gorgui Diouf : « Un monde où 1,4 milliard d’Africains n’ont pas de voix permanente est profondément injuste »
items.description: Alors que se déroule la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, sur fond de conflits persistants et de rivalités entre grandes puissances, Gorgui Diouf, Docteur en Droit public, spécialiste du droit international public, des relations internationales et de la géopolitique, également expert du droit onusien, porte un regard critique sur l’état du multilatéralisme. Dans cet entretien, il analyse les limites du système des Nations unies, la paralysie du Conseil de sécurité, les enjeux de sa réforme et la recomposition des rapports de force mondiaux. La 81e Assemblée générale de l’Onu s’ouvre dans un contexte de conflits multiples et de tensions entre grandes puissances. Quel état du monde cette rencontre va-t-elle, selon vous, mettre en lumière ? Cette 81e Assemblée générale des Nations unies va mettre en lumière un monde qui a perdu ses repères juridiques et moraux. Nous assistons à une forme de régression du droit international public. Les grands principes qui fondaient l’ordre mondial depuis 1945, tels que la sécurité collective et le règlement pacifique des différends (le chapitre VI et les articles 33 et 38 de la Charte), ainsi que l’interdiction du recours à la force (article 2, paragraphe 4), sont aujourd’hui piétinés par ceux-là mêmes qui devraient en être les garants. Le Conseil de sécurité est devenu le théâtre d’une confiscation de l’autorité juridique de l’Onu par les cinq membres permanents. Chacun utilise le droit de veto non pas pour protéger la paix, mais pour protéger ses intérêts géostratégiques. Résultat : les conflits comme celui du Sahel, du Soudan ou de l’est de la République démocratique du Congo s’enlisent et l’Onu assiste, impuissante, à la décomposition de régions entières. Cette Assemblée générale sera donc le miroir d’un monde où le droit n’est plus qu’un instrument au service de la puissance. Face à la multiplication des crises et aux difficultés du Conseil de sécurité, l’Onu dispose-t-elle encore des moyens politiques nécessaires pour peser réellement sur les grands conflits internationaux ? La réponse est non et il faut avoir le courage de le dire. L’Onu ne dispose plus des moyens politiques de sa mission parce que sa structure même est viciée à la racine. Dans le cadre de mes recherches, j’ai analysé en profondeur ce que j’appelle la « tare congénitale » du système onusien. La Charte de San Francisco a été rédigée en 1945 par les vainqueurs de la Seconde Guerre mondiale pour un monde qui n’existe plus. Elle n’a jamais prévu les conflits armés internes, les guerres civiles, les rébellions, les formes de terrorisme qui déchirent l’Afrique. L’Onu a dû bricoler des opérations de maintien de la paix qui n’ont aucune base juridique explicite dans la Charte. Et aujourd’hui, ces bricolages montrent leurs limites. Le Conseil de sécurité est paralysé par le veto. L’Assemblée générale est réduite à des recommandations sans force contraignante. Le Secrétaire général est un géant politique aux mains liées. L’Onu n’est pas impuissante par accident ; elle est impuissante par construction. Et cette impuissance est encore plus criante en Afrique où les conflits internes sont complexes, imprévisibles et où les puissances n’ont souvent aucun intérêt stratégique à agir. La réforme du Conseil de sécurité revient régulièrement. Peut-on s’attendre à des avancées concrètes, notamment en ce qui concerne la représentation de l’Afrique ? Il faut être lucide : il n’y aura pas d’avancée majeure cette année ni l’année prochaine. Les cinq membres permanents ne renonceront jamais volontairement à leur privilège. Le droit de veto est pour eux un attribut de souveraineté, un instrument de domination. L’Afrique le réclame depuis des décennies, mais elle se heurte à un mur. Cela dit, cette Assemblée générale est une occasion de plus pour le Sénégal et pour l’Union africaine de poser le problème en termes de justice et non de simple réforme technique. Il ne s’agit pas seulement de savoir qui siège au Conseil, mais de quel monde nous voulons. Un monde où 1,4 milliard d’Africains n’ont pas de voix permanente au Conseil de sécurité est un monde profondément injuste. Et cette injustice est une cause directe de l’instabilité sur notre continent. Tant que l’Afrique ne sera pas représentée dignement, les décisions sur la paix en Afrique seront prises sans les Africains et souvent contre eux. Dans un contexte de rivalités croissantes entre puissances occidentales, Chine, Russie et pays du Sud global, assiste-t-on à une recomposition durable des rapports de force au sein des Nations unies ? Oui, nous assistons à une recomposition historique. Le monde unipolaire dominé par les États-Unis est en train de céder la place à un monde multipolaire où la Chine, la Russie, l’Inde, le Brésil et les pays du Sud global pèsent de plus en plus. Mais, attention : multipolarité ne signifie pas automatiquement paix ou justice. Le risque, c’est que cette recomposition se fasse dans la confrontation, dans une nouvelle guerre froide qui utiliserait l’Afrique comme terrain d’affrontement. Le Sénégal, comme la plupart des pays africains, refuse d’être un pion dans ce jeu. Nous devons être des acteurs, pas des enjeux. C’est pourquoi la diplomatie sénégalaise doit être audacieuse, non alignée, mais pas neutre. Non alignée sur les blocs, mais fermement engagée pour le droit international, pour la justice et pour la paix. Au-delà de la paix et de la sécurité, le climat, le financement du développement et la gouvernance de l’Intelligence artificielle sont à l’agenda. Quels résultats concrets les pays africains peuvent-ils attendre ? Les attentes sont immenses, mais les résultats seront probablement décevants. Sur le climat, l’Afrique subit de plein fouet les conséquences d’un réchauffement qu’elle n’a pas causé. Les promesses de financement ne sont pas tenues. Sur le développement, l’architecture financière internationale est conçue pour maintenir les pays africains dans une dépendance structurelle. Sur l’Intelligence artificielle, l’Afrique risque d’être un simple marché pour les technologies des autres, sans maîtrise ni régulation. Toutefois, il y a une chose que les pays africains peuvent et doivent faire : exiger que ces questions soient traitées dans une logique de justice globale et non de charité. Le Sénégal doit porter une voix forte pour un financement climatique juste, pour une réforme de la gouvernance économique mondiale et pour une gouvernance de l’IA qui protège les droits humains et la souveraineté des peuples. Ces combats sont indissociables de la paix. Pour le Sénégal, quelles devraient être les priorités diplomatiques à cette tribune et quelle place le pays peut-il occuper dans les débats sur la réforme de la gouvernance mondiale ? Le Sénégal a une carte à jouer et il doit la jouer avec intelligence et courage. Sa première priorité, c’est de porter la voix de l’Afrique pour la réforme du Conseil de sécurité. Le Sénégal a une légitimité historique : il est un pays stable, démocratique, respecté, qui a toujours contribué aux opérations de maintien de la paix. Il doit être le fer de lance de cette bataille pour la justice institutionnelle. La deuxième priorité consiste à proposer une nouvelle approche de la sécurité au Sahel. Le Sénégal doit plaider pour une stratégie qui ne soit pas uniquement militaire, mais qui s’attaque aux causes profondes, à savoir la pauvreté, l’exclusion, le manque d’éducation. La troisième priorité, et c’est la plus profonde, est de faire du Sénégal le laboratoire d’une culture de la paix en Afrique. Le Sénégal a une richesse inestimable : sa culture de dialogue, de tolérance. Notre pays a une histoire de médiation, de dialogue pacifique. Il doit transformer cette richesse en une véritable diplomatie culturelle de la paix. Concrètement, cela signifie investir massivement dans l’éducation à la paix, dans la formation des jeunes, dans la promotion des valeurs de non-violence. « La paix ne se décrète pas à New York ; elle se construit dans les esprits », dans les écoles, dans les villages. Le Sénégal peut et doit être le pionnier de cette approche. · Entretien réalisé par Daouda DIOUF

items.title: Array of Experts Back Lawsuit Challenging Trump’s ICC Sanctions Regime
items.description: Click to expand Image Thurgood Marshall United States Federal Courthouse building in lower Manhattan, New York City. © 2026 Laura Prieto Uribe/Human Rights Watch (New York) – An array of former government officials, human rights groups, bar associations, and legal experts from around the world have filed eight amicus briefs supporting a lawsuit challenging US President Donald Trump’s executive order authorizing sanctions on International Criminal Court (ICC) officials, staff, and others affiliated with or assisting the court’s work. The American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute brought the suit on August 11, 2026. They subsequently sought a preliminary injunction to stop the sanctions, which they say illegally undermine access to justice for victims of serious international crimes and prevent civil society from working together to end impunity. The groups say in their suit that the sanctions are a blatantly illegal attack on international justice. The groups assert the sanctions have forced them to curtail a wide range of work in violation of their First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Their lawsuit also argues the sanctions exceed the president’s powers and are based on a false claim of a “national emergency,” arising out of the work of the ICC, that has no basis in fact. While the ICC has long been a target of opponents of international justice due to its investigations into atrocities, including in Libya, the Philippines, Sudan, and Ukraine, its Palestine investigation—which led to arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Minister of Defense Yoav Gallant and a Hamas official on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity—has sparked an escalated assault by the Trump administration on the institution and the rule of law. In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pledged to “dismantle” the court by, among other steps, increasing the use of sanctions. The administration has used the executive order to sanction ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges including the court’s president, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, and three leading Palestinian human rights groups. The following groups have filed the amicus briefs: A coalition of 38 human rights organizations, including Amnesty International and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), details how the ICC sanctions have impaired civil society from supporting international justice efforts. Former US sanctions officials, including in the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), articulate why the Trump administration’s use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act (IEEPA) is a dangerous departure and how it undermines the credibility and effectiveness of US sanctions. The Brennan Center for Justice explains why the executive order and the resulting sanctions exceed the president’s authority under the National Emergency Act and IEEPA. Physicians for Human Rights outlines how the ICC sanctions have made it more difficult for victims of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes to pursue and secure justice. Former US ambassadors-at-large for global criminal justice and prosecutors of international criminal tribunals discuss the importance of the ICC to international justice, the necessity of judicial and prosecutorial independence within the ICC, and the important role that civil society plays within the justice system.The International Criminal Court Bar Association (ICCBA) argues that the sanctions threaten to undermine the independence of ICC lawyers and therefore pose a grave threat to the rule of law. The New York City Bar Association (NYCBA) asserts that the ICC is an essential component of international justice and that the executive order undermines judicial independence, interferes with the work of the legal profession, and impairs the administration of justice.Legal academics, professors, and practitioners whose teaching, scholarship, and professional engagement focus on international law and related fields describe how the sanctions impair their ability to teach, conduct research, and collaborate within the international legal sphere; chill academic freedom; and violate their First Amendment rights. Plaintiffs are represented by Foley Hoag LLP.

Le Président Doumbouya après son retour à Conakry : « nos différences sont une richesse, jamais une fracture »
items.description: De retour à Conakry après sa participation à la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations Unies à New York, le président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, a adressé, ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026, un message de remerciement aux Guinéens, tout en appelant au renforcement de la cohésion sociale et du vivre-ensemble. Dans une publication publiée sur sa page Facebook, le chef de l’État est revenu sur l’accueil qui lui a été réservé à son arrivée dans la capitale. « Aujourd'hui, Conakry m'a offert l'une des plus belles émotions de ma vie. De l'aéroport jusqu'au cœur de la capitale, vous étiez là, par milliers, jeunes et anciens, femmes et hommes de toutes les régions, unis dans la même fierté », a-t-il écrit. Mamadi Doumbouya a également adressé ses remerciements aux Guinéens établis aux États-Unis pour la mobilisation dont ils ont fait preuve durant son séjour à New York. Le président de la République est ensuite revenu sur son intervention à la tribune de la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations Unies. Selon lui, le message porté à New York dépassait sa personne pour traduire les aspirations de la Guinée et, plus largement, celles d’une Afrique souhaitant définir ses propres modèles de développement. « À la tribune de la 81e session de l'Assemblée générale des Nations unies, ce n'est pas ma voix qui s'est fait entendre. C'est celle du peuple souverain de la République de Guinée, et au-delà, celle d'une Afrique qui refuse désormais les modèles imposés », a-t-il affirmé. Lors de son discours prononcé mercredi 23 septembre à New York, Mamadi Doumbouya avait notamment plaidé pour des modèles de gouvernance adaptés aux réalités historiques, sociales et culturelles des États africains, ainsi que pour une coopération internationale reposant sur le respect de la souveraineté et des partenariats « gagnant-gagnant ». Un appel au vivre-ensemble Dans son message publié à son retour, le chef de l’État a surtout insisté sur la nécessité de préserver l’unité nationale. Il appelle les Guinéens à dépasser leurs différences et à faire de la lutte contre la pauvreté une priorité commune. « Je vous appelle à renforcer la cohésion sociale et le vivre-ensemble, car la République de Guinée est une et indivisible. Nos différences sont une richesse, jamais une fracture. Le seul combat qui mérite d'être mené est celui contre la pauvreté », a déclaré Mamadi Doumbouya. Le président de la République invite enfin les Guinéens à poursuivre les efforts en faveur du développement socio-économique du pays et de l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. Ce message intervient au terme du séjour du chef de l’État à New York, où il a participé aux travaux de la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations Unies et multiplié les rencontres diplomatiques. Il s’est notamment entretenu, jeudi 24 septembre, avec le secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, autour de plusieurs questions liées à la paix, à la sécurité, à la gouvernance et au développement de la Guinée.

items.title: Xi sends letter to high-level dialogue marking 5th anniversary of GDI
items.description: Chinese President Xi Jinping has sent a congratulatory letter to a high-level dialogue marking the fifth anniversary of the Global Development Initiative (GDI), held at the UN headquarters in New York on Friday. Development is the eternal theme of human society and is key to promoting the well-being of humankind, Xi said. Xi recalled that he proposed the GDI at the UN General Assembly five years ago to advance global development cooperation, reinvigorate the global development cause, and help accelerate the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Over the past five years, with the joint efforts of all parties, the GDI has been widely implemented, with cooperation projects under the initiative taking root and yielding outcomes in more than 120 countries, writing a new chapter of common development and win-win cooperation, Xi noted. Xi pointed out that nowadays, changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the world, and people in all countries are more eager for development. As the world's largest developing country and a member of the Global South, China stands ready to work with all parties to uphold a people-centered development philosophy, advance the GDI, turn the vision of the Sustainable Development Goals into reality, and make new and greater contributions to building a community with a shared future for humanity, Xi said. (Cover: African scholars visit a smart blueberry cultivation facility in Jinhua, east China's Zhejiang Province, May 23, 2026. /VCG)

items.title: Opoku Mensah urges Christian Council, House of Chiefs to speak up on democratic freedoms
items.description: Spokesperson for former Education Minister Dr Yaw Osei Adutwum has challenged the Christian Council of Ghana and the National House of Chiefs to speak out on what he describes as the erosion of democratic freedoms in Ghana. According to Yaw Opoku Mensah, the two institutions, as important moral voices in the country, have a responsibility to speak when citizens’ rights and freedoms are at stake. He expressed concern over what he described as the government’s resort to the arrest of dissenting voices, arguing that such developments raise questions about the protection of democratic freedoms. “The Christian Council and the National House of Chiefs are supposed to be moral voices of the country and as institutions capable of speaking truth to power when citizens’ rights and freedoms are at stake,” he said. According to him, the apparent silence of such institutions should not always be interpreted as neutrality. “Silence cannot always be called neutrality. Sometimes, silence is a betrayal,” Mr Opoku Mensah said. He questioned the role of the two institutions if concerns about being perceived as supporting a particular political side prevented them from speaking against the alleged abuse of state power. “If fear of being accused of supporting one political side prevents these institutions from speaking when government power is being abused, then we must ask: who exactly are they representing?” he asked. Mr Mensah stressed that accountability should apply to every government, regardless of the political party in power. “Government must be held accountable, regardless of which political party is in power. Human rights do not belong to any political party. They belong to the Ghanaian people,” he said. He further warned that Ghana’s democracy could face serious challenges if institutions expected to serve as the country’s moral conscience fail to speak when necessary. “If the institutions that should serve as the moral conscience of the nation cannot call power to order when necessary, then our democracy has a serious problem,” he said. Mr Mensah therefore called for what he described as moral courage from the two institutions. “Ghana needs moral courage, not convenient silence. Speak up when it matters,” he added.

items.title: Législatives au Maroc : miracle au royaume désenchanté
items.description: Les résultats des élections législatives au Maroc réservent toujours des surprises. Au Sahara occidental occupé, la démocratie a fait un bond quantique pendant que le reste du Maroc, lui, restait sagement en retrait. 77 % de participation à Laâyoune contre 38 % dans le Royaume ! Statistiquement, c'est moins une élection qu'un miracle liturgique. On nous sert cette prouesse comme une preuve d'amour spontané pour l'isoloir, dans une région où le simple mot « référendum » fait tousser l'ONU depuis 1975. Étrange, cette ferveur électorale précisément là où la question posée (à qui appartient ce territoire ?) n'a jamais eu le droit d'être soumise, elle, au vote populaire. Le tour de passe-passe est d'ailleurs bien huilé. Prenez un corps électoral façonné depuis des décennies par une colonisation de peuplement assumée, ajoutez une pincée d'« observateurs internationaux » soigneusement invités, saupoudrez de huit députées « sahraouies » exhibées comme des trophées de vertu progressiste, et voilà, le bulletin de vote devient un certificat de souveraineté, validé par visa diplomatique. Le clou du spectacle reste ce contraste : pendant que Rabat et Casablanca haussent les épaules devant les urnes, Laâyoune, elle, se précipiterait aux bureaux de vote avec la ferveur d'un converti de la dernière heure. Une mise en scène bien rodée Il faudrait être bien naïf pour ne pas y voir autre chose qu'une mise en scène rodée, où la participation record sert moins à élire des députés qu'à faire taire, une fois de plus, la question du Sahara occidental occupé à coups de pourcentages fictifs. Un vote sincère ne se mesure pas au nombre de mains levées quand on a soigneusement choisi qui avait le droit d'être dans la salle. Allez chiche ! Organisez le référendum d’autodétermination. *Ancien Ambassadeur L’article Législatives au Maroc : miracle au royaume désenchanté est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: The Right Way to Adapt a Video Game
items.description: The moment I knew Resident Evil had me was the ammo check. The protagonist of the director Zach Cregger’s new film is a civilian, a medical courier named Bryan (played by Austin Abrams) who’s been tasked with driving a special package over to nearby Raccoon City in the snow. Quickly enough, strange things start to happen: He almost runs over a woman who seems to be sick with a mysterious virus; as the situation disintegrates, he finds himself fending her off with a dead police officer’s pistol. Amidst all the chaos, Bryan slides out his gun’s magazine to count how many bullets he has left. Confirming how many rounds are in the chamber before venturing further into the darkness is a key aspect of the video-game series that Cregger is adapting. But rarely is that ever shown on the big screen. Indeed, the seven Resident Evil films that were made before this one (all but one of which starred Milla Jovovich) took the opposite approach. The characters toted comical varieties of automatic weapons, possessed supernatural abilities, performed amazing vehicular stunts, and pumped thousands of bullets into waves of zombies. The new film’s comparative groundedness is perhaps why Cregger’s initial pitch for a fresh iteration of Resident Evil , one of the best-known video-game properties, resonated with Constantin Films, which holds the rights. “I like the idea of somebody with my skill set and my attitude going into this world,” Cregger told me in an interview of that storytelling choice—that is, turning an unassuming young man whose primary concerns include his girlfriend and his sneakers into a mutant-slaying hero. The director chose not to draw from a specific entry of the game series, which debuted in 1996. Cregger is best known for his first feature film, Barbarian , which announced him as a surprising new talent in the horror world, and for his follow-up, Weapons , which won an Oscar. For his current film, capturing the stressful sensation of actually playing the game was important to him. “ Resident Evil is so simple and so inherently cinematic,” Cregger said, noting that he himself plays it “because the game design and the pacing and the dread is so effective. That, to me, is the heart and soul of those games. It is the feeling you get when you walk into a new environment, and you only have two bullets.” Managing resources, making every shot count, and navigating a world where a monster could jump out from behind any corner—they’re fundamental to the feel of this world, he said. Resident Evil helped create the wildly popular gaming genre known as survival horror, which mixes suspense and action to hook the player. But as with almost any sprawling franchise, it has become burdened by years of continuity. Cregger solves this problem by ignoring most of the backstory for his version. The essential premise is still there: A pharma-bio conglomerate, the Umbrella Corporation, has mistakenly unleashed something called the “T-Virus,” transforming those who are infected into monsters that Bryan must combat in the hopes of survival. The source material usually foregrounds members of law enforcement, most of whom have been featured in past screen adaptations, but Cregger chose to focus on an original character. Bryan fills the role of the average person behind the controller, who’s entered a hostile world barely able to defend himself—forcing him to translate into reality what he’s learned by playing video games. [ Read: A boring video game I can’t put down ] The result is a rollicking, often ridiculous viewing experience, as Bryan hits some lucky shots early on but also makes some rookie mistakes. In one sequence supercharged with video-game logic, he foolishly discards a ladder that could have obviously helped him escape an attic he’s stuck in; in another, he evades a zombie attacker by simply running in circles around an overturned car. As he progresses, Bryan levels up his arsenal, coming across a shotgun and then an automatic weapon. Cregger’s homage to a nasty element of later Resident Evil installments (namely the fourth, which he has called one of his all-time favorite games) is especially amusing: Executing a headshot to kill an enemy can actually be detrimental , as some new tentacled horror might sprout from the neck wound. Bryan’s situation is so absurdly terrifying that laughing as it escalates is inevitable. Humor is, of course, the best way to defuse tension or deflate shocking gore; that’s especially true in moments such as Bryan confronting an infected child or a maternity ward full of mutated babies. Cregger started his career as one of the members of the sketch group the Whitest Kids U’ Know, and his previous movies have a darkly funny edge. He also admitted that the Resident Evil games themselves have “a camp to them that’s undeniable.” Yet Cregger seemed to regret the amount of humor he’d deployed in his take—and that was despite the fact that he’d already pulled some jokes out in the editing process. He had run out the clock, having “turned the movie in at, like, 11:59 p.m. a week before it hit theaters,” he said. Still, he recounted, while watching the finished film, he was thinking, “ I could have lost that; I could have cut that .” He’d also done plenty of big edits, other than just culling lines; the climax, in which Bryan makes it to his destination (a fortified Umbrella lab working on a cure to the virus), in particular changed drastically over time. The scene is filled with comedic actors playing frazzled lab attendants, and initially came across as more outwardly zany. “I had to go and make some really painful cuts to some really great performances and funny, clever things that people were doing in that lab and try and keep it hard-core,” Cregger said. Given the audience’s emotional investment in Bryan’s journey up to that point, however, he realized that they would “not really be in the mood to be chuckling at clever quips that the lab dudes are telling.” To me, though, the humor matches the odd and dissonant tone of some video games, and is thus part of the appeal. The way the film moves through scenes that feel akin to “levels” without feeling schematic was also impressive. Bryan’s first major challenge is at the site of a car crash, after which he trudges to an abandoned house nearby; then he moves through the streets and sewers of Raccoon City, before making it to the lab. Cregger replicates in a way that feels organic the Resident Evil games’ tendency to move players from place to place quickly. [ Read: The Last of Us and the power of video games ] It became obvious how much of a Resident Evil super-fan Cregger is as he referenced detailed aspects of the games that inspired him. (The fairly straightforward path Bryan’s journey takes was another Resident Evil 4 homage, for instance.) Indeed, the entire project came about when he was asked by the film’s producer Roy Lee, who had worked on the Minecraft movie , whether Cregger would ever be interested in adapting a video game. “The only one I could think of would be Resident Evil ,” he said, because he felt that no film had quite yet captured the spirit of playing it. Nevertheless, he faced backlash online from fans for eschewing the franchise’s established characters and plot—a sense of skepticism from a community that often sees their favorite games clunkily translated to the big screen. Cregger was unsurprised. “I was expecting, as D-Day was approaching, I’m gonna get shredded,” he said. “I was already getting shredded by the people who were supposed to like the movie. So, I was just like, well, this is just gonna be the humbling that I am due for.” Instead, the film has been a colossal success for the Resident Evil franchise, earning strong reviews and grossing more in its opening weekend—upwards of $60 million domestically—than any prior adaptation made in its entire U.S. box-office run.Theatergoers, who now comprise multiple generations of video-game fans, have responded to the film’s atmosphere; they’ve never encountered cinema that so closely resembles their side of the player equation. The connection to the source material does matter to Cregger, of course: “The one thing that I really hate is the accusation that I’ve been getting that I just want to make a movie and slap Resident Evil on it,” he said. “This was always supposed to be Resident Evil .” But adapting the franchise doesn’t have to mean engaging with the lore—it can be as simple as capturing a feeling.

items.title: Kissidougou : l’axe Faranah–Kissidougou coupée après l’effondrement d’un pont à Sangardo
items.description: La circulation routière est totalement interrompue ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026 sur la Route nationale n°2 (RN2), reliant Faranah à Kissidougou, précisément dans la sous-préfecture de Sangardo, à environ 25 kilomètres du centre-ville de Kissidougou. Cette interruption fait suite à l’effondrement d’un pont qui présentait déjà d’importantes dégradations depuis plus d’un mois. Fragilisé au fil des jours, l’ouvrage a finalement cédé ce vendredi matin, sous l’effet des intempéries et de la forte pression des eaux. Selon les informations recueillies sur place, le pont était déjà fortement endommagé et son état suscitait de vives inquiétudes chez les usagers de cet axe stratégique. La dégradation progressive de l’ouvrage faisait craindre une rupture de la circulation. Ces craintes se sont finalement concrétisées ce vendredi matin avec l’effondrement du pont, rendant impossible le passage des véhicules. Des véhicules bloqués La rupture de l’ouvrage a entraîné une coupure totale du trafic sur ce tronçon de la RN2. Des véhicules de transport en commun, des camions et de nombreux autres usagers se sont retrouvés bloqués de part et d’autre du pont, dans l’attente d’une éventuelle solution. Cette situation constitue une nouvelle difficulté pour les usagers de cet axe reliant Faranah à Kissidougou, particulièrement fréquenté par les transporteurs et les populations des localités riveraines. Pour l’heure, aucune solution permettant de rétablir la circulation n’a encore été annoncée. Les usagers attendent désormais une intervention rapide des services compétents afin de sécuriser les lieux et de mettre en place, dans les meilleurs délais, un dispositif provisoire permettant de rétablir le trafic sur cet important axe routier.

items.title: Produits agricoles : Un investissement de 175 milliards envisagé pour renforcer le mécanisme de stockage
items.description: Dans le cadre de la planification, de la transformation et de la commercialisation des produits agricoles et d’élevage, le gouvernement du Sénégal envisage de faire du stockage une de ses priorités. Un important lot d’équipements de stockage, dont des chambres froides seront livrés d’ici à la fin de l’année, à Fass Boye et à Sangalkam. L’annonce a été faite, ce vendredi, par Serigne Guèye Diop, ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce. Il est également annoncé un investissement de 175 milliards de francs CFA dans les infrastructures de stockage, dans le but de pouvoir et stocker 250 000 tonnes de produits agricoles par an. M. Diop annonce également la mise en place d’une caisse de péréquation et de stabilisation du prix du riz local. Le mécanisme sera alimenté par un prélèvement de 8 FCFA sur chaque kilogramme de riz importé commercialisé au Sénégal. Selon le ministre de l’Industrie et du Commerce, ce mécanisme devrait générer entre 13 et 15 milliards de FCFA par an. Ces ressources permettraient de soutenir la filière rizicole nationale et, notamment, de contribuer à maintenir le prix du riz local à un niveau inférieur à celui du riz importé. L’objectif affiché est de créer un mécanisme de soutien permettant de mieux réguler le prix du riz local et de renforcer sa compétitivité face aux produits importés. O.BA

items.title: Moussa Gningue : Le « Sorcier de Fass » a consacré 45 ans à l’écurie
items.description: Certains acteurs ont marqué l’arène par leurs exploits avant de se réinventer ou de se reconvertir après leur carrière. La rubrique « Que sont-ils devenus ? » raconte leur vie d’après-carrière. Aujourd’hui, coup de projecteur sur Moussa Gningue, l’emblématique ancien préparateur mystique de Mbaye Guèye, de son frère Moustapha Guèye et de Gris Bordeaux, qui a désormais passé le témoin à ses héritiers. Dans l’arène, certains combattent à mains nues, d’autres travaillent dans l’ombre. Moussa Gningue a été de ceux dont la présence précédait les grands combats des sociétaires de l’écurie mythique de Fass. Derrière Mbaye Guèye, Tapha Guèye, Gris Bordeaux et autres, il était l’homme des préparations mystiques. Son nom s’est ainsi forgé une réputation mêlée de respect, de crainte et de mystère. Pendant près d’un demi-siècle, Moussa Gningue a vécu au cœur de la mythique écurie Fass. Il y a occupé une place singulière, celle de préparateur mystique, conseiller et homme de confiance aux côtés des trois « Tigres » de Fass : Mbaye Guèye, Tapha Guèye et Gris Bordeaux. Sa présence dans l’entourage des champions alimentait la curiosité et parfois la crainte de leurs adversaires. Surnommé le « Sorcier de Fass », il revendique 45 années d’expérience dans ce domaine, voire plus, et raconte les pratiques mystiques qui ont accompagné plusieurs générations de lutteurs. Il n’est donc pas faux de dire que pendant des décennies, son visage a été indissociable de celui des grands champions de Fass. Il occupait une place à part. C’est sa réputation qui lui a effectivement valu ce surnom de « Sorcier de Fass », tant son nom était associé aux préparations mystiques précédant les grands combats. Dans l’intimité des champions Né et ayant grandi à Fass, il revendique une appartenance profonde à ce quartier et à cette famille sportive. Il a passé plusieurs années dans l’univers de la lutte, après y être entré à l’âge de 15 ans. Il répétait souvent qu’il pouvait quitter l’enceinte, mais jamais l’écurie Fass. Avant de devenir une figure de proue connue du mystique dans le landerneau de la lutte sénégalaise, Moussa Gningue avait également fréquenté le football. Il raconte avoir joué à la Jeanne d’Arc de Dakar, au Jaraaf et à l’Us Rail. Il a aussi travaillé à l’Oncad. Des expériences qui ont contribué à l’ancrer davantage dans le milieu sportif dakarois. Son histoire avec Fass s’est surtout écrite aux côtés de plusieurs générations de lutteurs. Il a accompagné Mbaye Guèye, premier « Tigre de Fass », puis Tapha Guèye et Gris Bordeaux. Il se souvient des longues préparations précédant les grands combats, les déplacements à travers le Sénégal et la sous-région, mais aussi de ses relations avec différents marabouts. Avec Mbaye Guèye, la relation dépassait le cadre d’une simple préparation. Moussa Gningue décrit un champion emblématique qui travaillait durement sur le plan physique tout en accordant une place importante aux pratiques mystiques. « Mbaye Guèye pesait entre 75 et 80 kg. Il s’entraînait d’arrache-pied. Cela ne l’empêchait pas de faire des pratiques mystiques. Il se rendait à Banjul, en Casamance, au Mali et dans beaucoup d’autres pays de la sous-région pour ses protections. Il est vrai que le 1er « Tigre de Fass » était très talentueux et teigneux, mais il ne négligeait vraiment pas l’aspect mystique. Il était convaincu que cela faisait partie de cette activité sportive », reconnaît-il, les souvenirs vifs. À l’en croire, « le mystique est un aspect important dans la lutte. C’est dans le milieu de la lutte qu’on sent le plus son efficacité. Mais, le lutteur doit apprendre à lutter et être physiquement au top. Le mystique constitue la troisième force d’un lutteur. Cela ne veut pas dire qu’il est à sous-estimer ». Avec l’expérience, il estime que « le mystique, nous l’avons hérité de nos arrière-grands-parents. Ils avaient de fortes croyances mystiques ». Il affirme également avoir « une fois entendu Yékini confirmer l’importance du mystique dans ce sport ». L’ancien Roi des arènes disait qu’un athlète ne pouvait pas être techniquement doué sans faire de pratiques mystiques, en se fondant sur sa propre expérience. Au cours de sa longue carrière de préparateur mystique, Moussa Gningue dit avoir été témoin de faits pour le moins surprenants. Il raconte notamment une scène survenue lors de la préparation du légendaire combat entre Mbaye Guèye et Sa Ndiambour. « Lors de son combat contre Sa Ndiambour, Mbaye Guèye faisait quelques séances d’entraînement en boxe dans la main courante. Un photographe s’était approché de lui alors qu’il était en train de lancer des coups dans le vide. Subitement, l’air que le « 1er Tigre » produisait au moment de lancer ses coups avait emporté ce photographe qui s’était évanoui ». Autre souvenir marquant : le combat entre le même Mbaye Guèye et Boy Bambara. Anecdotes fascinantes « Un marabout nous avait donné des substances à bouillir. Il avait dit à Mbaye Guèye que s’il les faisait chauffer avant 16 heures, le combat ne se tiendrait pas. Nous n’avions pas suivi ses conseils et avions fait bouillir lesdites matières vers 12 heures. Et avant 14 heures, l’information selon laquelle Boy Bambara n’allait pas combattre était tombée. Du jamais-vu ! », révèle-t-il, stupéfait. Après la retraite de Mbaye Guèye, Moussa Gningue a été chargé de l’accompagnement mystique de son jeune frère Moustapha Guèye. Ce dernier se concentrait davantage sur les entraînements. « Sur le plan mystique, c’est moi qui lui dictais la conduite à tenir », renseigne-t-il. D’après son témoignage, Moustapha Guèye bénéficiait également du soutien de certaines personnalités de l’État, qui contribuaient financièrement à ses préparations spirituelles ou ésotériques. L’ancien président de l’écurie Fass Momar Ndiaye l’aidait également dans ce domaine. Après Moustapha Guèye, il a poursuivi sa mission auprès de Gris Bordeaux, officiellement intronisé « 3e Tigre de Fass », à l’occasion du jubilé de Moustapha Guèye le 8 août 2010 au stade Demba Diop. En 2011, Moussa Gningue racontait notamment l’importance qu’il avait accordée au combat Gris Bordeaux–Bombardier, disputé le 22 juillet 2007, au point d’y consacrer des moyens considérables. Il expliquait alors avoir parfois dépensé le double, voire le triple, des sommes qui lui étaient confiées pour les préparatifs. Le jour du combat, Gris Bordeaux avait pris le dessus sur le « B52 de Mbour », déclenchant une immense liesse dans l’arène et à Fass. Une victoire à laquelle Moussa Gningue estime avoir contribué à sa manière. L’affiche qui avait polarisé toutes les passions reste encore gravée dans la mémoire des amateurs. Les années passant, Moussa Gningue a choisi de s’écarter de l’arène. Il expliquait avoir décidé de se retirer après plusieurs décennies de présence, notamment en raison de désaccords internes et d’évolutions de l’écurie qui ne correspondaient plus à sa vision. Mais, quitter les préparations mystiques ne signifie pas tourner le dos à Fass, qu’on pourrait considérer comme la seule et unique entité de lutte de sa vie. Pour les dignitaires de l’écurie, Moussa Gningue demeure « un conseiller dont l’expérience mérite d’être transmise à la nouvelle génération ». Un certain Thierno Diop avait d’abord pris le relais avant de se retirer à son tour. Moussa Gningue a ensuite confié cette mission à ses enfants. C’est l’une des particularités de son parcours : la transmission. Une retraite sans rupture Il nous révèle que ses enfants ont accepté d’accompagner Madiagne Guèye, fils de Tapha Guèye, surnommé « Fils de Tigre ». Il leur avait expliqué qu’ils l’avaient longtemps accompagné dans ses déplacements auprès des marabouts. « Je faisais le travail avec deux de mes héritiers. Ce sont des intellectuels, mais je partais avec eux chez des marabouts », affirme-t-il. L’objectif, poursuit-il, « était qu’ils puissent, eux aussi, avoir des potions et des amulettes et en faire un usage personnel. Je ne partais donc jamais seul. Je me débrouillais pour avoir à mes côtés, au moins, un de mes enfants ». Même éloigné des premiers rôles, Moussa Gningue continue ainsi de laisser son empreinte dans l’arène. Son héritage ne se résume pas aux histoires mystérieuses racontées autour des grands combats de Fass. Il est aussi celui d’un homme qui aura consacré une grande partie de son existence à une écurie dont il revendique toujours l’identité. À l’heure où une nouvelle génération prend progressivement le relais, le « Sorcier de Fass » demeure une mémoire vivante de l’écurie. Un témoin d’une époque où les grands combats de lutte se préparaient autant dans les salles d’entraînement que dans les coulisses, loin des regards du grand public. Par Abdoulaye DEMBÉLÉ

items.title: Plastiques à usage unique : l’Union pour la défense des consommateurs plaide pour un moratoire d’un an
items.description: Quelques jours après l’entrée en vigueur de l’interdiction de certaines catégories de plastique à usage unique en Guinée, l’Union pour la défense des consommateurs de Guinée (UDCG) demande au gouvernement de surseoir à l’application de la mesure pour une période d’un an. Dans une plaidoirie adressée au président de la République et au Premier ministre, l’organisation estime que l’application de cette interdiction, effective depuis le 20 septembre 2026, entraîne des difficultés pour les consommateurs, notamment dans l’accès à l’eau potable et aux eaux minérales conditionnées dans les emballages concernés. Selon l’UDCG, les alternatives disponibles sur les marchés, dans les boutiques et dans les autres points de vente restent insuffisantes pour répondre aux besoins de la population. L’organisation relève également une hausse des prix de certaines eaux minérales, dans un contexte marqué par des difficultés d’approvisionnement en eau potable dans plusieurs zones. Pour l’UDCG, cette situation soulève également des préoccupations en matière de santé publique, l’accès à une eau de qualité demeurant une nécessité essentielle. L’organisation de défense des consommateurs propose ainsi une période transitoire d’un an, destinée, notamment, à permettre la mise en place de solutions alternatives accessibles et à renforcer les mécanismes de collecte et de traitement des déchets plastiques. L’UDCG affirme par ailleurs vouloir contribuer à l’élaboration d’un document destiné au gouvernement sur les questions liées à l’environnement, à l’assainissement et à la gestion des déchets plastiques. Elle annonce également sa participation aux actions de sensibilisation et d’accompagnement des autorités locales, pour améliorer la collecte et le traitement de ces déchets. À travers cette démarche, l’organisation dit défendre une transition écologique progressive, reposant sur des dispositifs structurels de collecte, de traitement et de gestion des déchets plastiques. L’UDCG annonce enfin qu’elle saisira plusieurs institutions républicaines afin de plaider en faveur d’un report d’un an, de l’application du décret présidentiel et de l’arrêté conjoint concernés.

items.title: Patrick Vieira après Mozambique-Sénégal : « Il y a des axes de progression, on doit continuer à travailler»
items.description: Accroché par le Mozambique ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026 à Maputo pour l'entame des qualifications à la CAN 2027, le Sénégal n'a pas réussi à confirmer sur la durée une première période pourtant maîtrisée. En conférence de presse d'après-match, Patrick Vieira, pour ses grands débuts sur le banc des Lions, a livré une analyse lucide, entre satisfaction et frustration. Le sélectionneur franco-sénégalais a d'abord tenu à saluer l'équilibre de son groupe, où jeunes pousses et cadres cohabitent. « Les jeunes, ils sont sélectionnés parce qu'ils ont du talent, ils ont démontré avec leur club respectif qu'ils avaient des qualités pour pouvoir prétendre jouer avec l'équipe nationale. La chance de ces jeunes, c'est qu'ils sont aussi encadrés par des joueurs avec de l'expérience. Ces joueurs d'expérience prennent leurs responsabilités dans les vestiaires pour les guider justement », a-t-il expliqué, avant de revenir sur l'ambiance qui règne au sein du groupe depuis sa prise de fonction. Lire aussi : Sénégal-Mozambique (1-1) : les Lions de Vieira, entre promesses et impression de déjà-vu Une première période aboutie, une seconde à corriger Pour son premier match officiel à la tête des Lions, Patrick Vieira dit avoir vu ce qu'il espérait, au moins pendant quarante-cinq minutes. « J'ai dit auparavant que j'étais vraiment satisfait de l'ambiance qu'il y avait au sein de l'équipe. Et ça s'est traduit aussi, surtout sur cette première période, avec cette cohérence et cette qualité de jeu sur cette première période. Bien sûr, il y a des regrets parce que ce que j'ai vu surtout sur cette première période, les joueurs, l'équipe méritaient mieux. » Mais le technicien n'élude pas les manques qui ont coûté deux points à son équipe. « Malheureusement, ça montre aussi qu' il y a des axes de progression, on doit continuer à travailler. On savait que tout n'allait pas être parfait sur ce match-là, on a identifié bien sûr les manques et ces manques-là, on va les combler avec le travail. Mais c'était important justement de construire ces fondations. » Rendez-vous le 29 septembre, lors du déplacement en Ethiopie, pour voir si Patrick Vieira et ses joueurs sauront cette fois remporter le match. O.B.N
